issues.body:
This issue collects the design of the new update path: what has landed, what is in progress, and who owns which part. It is meant as the shared reference for everyone working on updates, so we stop colliding on the same files with different designs.

## Goal

A user opens Settings in the Control UI and clicks Update. Within minutes the Gateway serves the new build, or it keeps serving the old build and the UI says why. No terminal, no manual step, no false "succeeded", no stuck Gateway.

## Why the old path keeps breaking

Root-cause analysis of about 2,700 upgrade failure reports (2026-11-15/17):

1. **In-place replacement of the running install was the largest cause** (about 600 field failures). The old updater stops the Gateway, swaps the package and runs checks while nothing serves.
2. **The installed old updater drives every upgrade.** Every fix needs one copy in the updater and another on the candidate side for older updaters. `docs/install/updating.md` carries dozens of "the installed updater must contain this fix" notes for this reason.
3. **It is slow.** Average update about 23 minutes with about 5.7 minutes of downtime. Pre-switch checks run while the Gateway is down took about 42% of update time.

The code swap itself almost never failed. The work around it did.

## The design

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Prepared releases** | Each update installs into its own `releases/<id>/` folder while the old Gateway keeps serving. Built on the release folders and link switch from #198835 (@fuller-stack-dev) and the proposal in #197949. |
| **Resident launcher** | The service always starts the launcher, never a release path. The launcher picks the active release. |
| **Trial with switch-back** | The new release starts once as a trial. If it fails to start twice, the launcher switches back to the previous release and restores its `.pre-<generation>` state files. |
| **The new release finishes its own update** | The old updater only prepares and checks. Activation, verification, plugins and the final result run in the new release's code, so a fix ships with the release that carries it. |
| **State copy-and-swap at first start** | The new Gateway migrates a private copy of the state, validates it and switches to it (#198389). The old state stays untouched for rollback. PostgreSQL uses the same model through a private namespace copy (#204502). |
| **Doctor is advisory** | It runs after the Gateway is listening. It never gates or rolls back an update. |

Measured on Linux and macOS after the switch: a normal update takes 2–3 minutes with 7–17 s of outage.

## What landed

- Git installs on prepared releases: #199706, #200578, #203194.
- npm, pnpm and Bun installs on prepared releases, with the old Gateway serving during preparation: #203497.
- Fixes from real-host testing: #203735 (containers and the official image), #203769 (no systemd user bus), #203504 (consent survives the restart; wrong-install refusal), #203990 (faster switch-back after a stalled start), #203994 (Doctor findings after success), #204054 (plain rollback message), #204094 (Windows state databases), #204127 (plugins update after the new Gateway is ready), #204215, #204515 (`npm i -g` then `gateway restart` applies the new version), #204502 (PostgreSQL copy-and-swap).
- Interim-snapshot recovery for Git checkouts on 2026-11-17–19 `main`: #201463, #201538, #204275, #204322, #204676.

## In progress: one owner per bug class

Instead of one fix per report, the remaining work is grouped into four classes. Each class gets one owner change.

| Class | Problem | The one change | PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Proof** | The release path merged before it had a real `T → T+1` run with a schema change on every platform | One CI lane: build `T` and `T+1` from the same source with a fixture-only schema step, and prove trial and rollback | #204685 |
| **B. One writer for the update result** | Several places write an update's final status: the old Gateway in process, a guess from process ID and uptime in `announceReady`, and the early-release recovery from #204322 | Before activation, `prepareUpdate` records refusals and preparation failures. After activation, one function at Gateway ready derives the final result from the lock and the trial. Every other writer is removed. Restart and health waits end on a committed trial, report "connected without operator scope" as its own outcome, and always have a deadline (#204704). | #204700 |
| **C. One state inventory, refuse before the stop** | Some databases fall outside the copy (#204394, #204227). Very large stores can exceed the trial budget. PostgreSQL stores that are too large migrate in place. | `discoverDatabases` becomes the single inventory. Everything the new release migrates is in the copy set, or the update refuses before the old Gateway stops, with the reason. The in-place PostgreSQL branch is removed. Normal startup outside an update still migrates as before. | #204752 |
| **D. Only the launcher is named after conversion** | Other installers and routes can bypass the launcher or take over the release slot: #204516, #203807, #204266 | After conversion, `gateway install` writes the launcher. Local routes that would fall through to the old in-place code refuse with a reason and a next step. Every service that runs the package is restarted through its owner or named in the result. | queued after B |

Before the next stable freezes the launcher and trial format, we also:
- pin that frozen contract with one test: trial fields, launcher IPC messages, exit 78, and the `.pre-<generation>` scan;
- keep the second start attempt (real launchd restarts during the trial needed it);
- refuse before the stop when the estimated state upgrade will not fit the trial budget, on SQLite and PostgreSQL.

## Test matrix before stable

Linux, macOS and Windows × npm and Git:
- `T → T+1` Control UI click with a schema bump;
- crash after migration;
- hang before listening;
- kill during prepare;
- reboot during the trial;
- first update from 2026.11.7.

Windows 11 runs from 2026.11.7 are required: #200756 reproduces on Windows 11 but not on Windows Server.

## What the old updater still has to do

The first update from any already-installed version is driven by that version's updater. Neither the new code nor a fix on `main` can change that. Until the oldest supported upgrade base contains the new path:

- **Fixes to the old updater belong on the release branches** that users will update from, for that first update. Examples: the pnpm fixes in #203401 and #204716.
- **On `main`, the old in-place code is frozen.** Change it only to land a fix that is ported to a release branch.
- **The old updater is deleted** once the oldest supported upgrade base includes #203497.

## Ownership

- **New update path on `main`:** `src/update/`, the launcher, `src/state/state-upgrade*` and run settlement. Changes go through the class owners above.
- **First updates from shipped versions:** release-branch fixes for the installed updaters (@fuller-stack-dev).
- **Design changes** to anything in the table above get raised here first.

## Open design questions

- **#201716 proposes in-place state migration at start** to avoid the copy's disk cost: about 70 GiB to copy with about 100 GiB free. The space problem is real. In-place migration loses rollback after a crash, though: of 98 schema steps in our history, 68 cannot be read by the previous release. Proposal: class C refuses before the stop when the copy will not fit. #201716 becomes a class C test case.
- **Windows:** outage on #204704's run was 82 s, against 7–17 s on Linux and macOS. Not yet explained.

## Open issues tracked here

#203764, #203807, #203628, #204394, #204516, #204227, #204704, #200756, #204266

## Reproduction

I reproduced this on Linux with a published OpenClaw 2026.9.37 Gateway and a real OpenAI-backed automation:

1. Configure gateway-host exec with allowlist/on-miss approval policy.
2. Create an isolated agent-turn automation that runs `/usr/bin/printf 'standing-grant-probe\n'` without an environment override.
3. Choose Always allow on the first occurrence. The next occurrence runs without prompting.
4. Stop the Gateway, run current-main Doctor against the same saved state, and start main at `277b251bfa80c863e4408607bce9b372eddc24c9`.
5. Run the unchanged automation again.

Expected: the existing standing grant still authorizes the exact command.

Actual: a new approval appears with `TEMP`, `TMP`, and `TMPDIR` in its environment keys. I declined it and confirmed the command did not run.

## Cause

Commit f91bc9900e813a80f084ef9ca29a890b827af006 (#202074) added runtime scratch defaults to the requested environment. That environment is hashed into both grant creation and lookup, so the old operation binding no longer matches. Runtime-owned scratch defaults should stay out of that binding; explicit environment overrides must remain bound.

This reproduction used a stopped-Gateway package-to-source transition with Doctor, not the built-in updater.

issues.body:
### Summary
Allow a plugin's `before_model_request` result to carry a small, explicitly gated set of outbound HTTP headers for embedded model requests.

### Problem to solve
`before_model_request` can rewrite the request body but not the transport headers. Integrations that route requests by their metadata need per-request values that only the plugin can compute at call time: which conversation this is, how many turns have already been sent, whether this call continues a tool loop, and how large the prefix is.

Today the only supported knob is static `models.providers.*.headers` / `request.headers`, which is identical on every call. `compat.sendSessionAffinityHeaders` covers a fixed set of affinity headers derived from `options.sessionId`, but not computed values. #16387 covers placeholder interpolation of `{{session.key}}` / `{{agent.id}}` / `{{run.id}}`; that cannot express "message count" or "is this a tool continuation".

### Proposed solution
`PluginHookBeforeModelRequestResult` gains `headers?: Record<string, string>`.

- Only `x-`-prefixed names (lowercase, `[a-z0-9-]`, ≤64 chars), values ≤4 KiB, no CR/LF/NUL. Anything else is dropped, never an error.
- Merged over provider defaults after the payload is admitted. Host-owned headers cannot be overridden: `authorization`, `content-type`, `host`, `anthropic-*`, `x-api-key`, …
- Multiple hooks compose by merging headers (`{ ...previous, ...next }`), not by letting the last hook's whole result win.
- Gated by a new capability flag in the hook metadata (e.g. `outboundHeaders: true`), so existing plugins do not silently gain the authority; `registry-registrars` keeps enforcing it.
- Ignored on `runtime: "cli"`, which owns its own wire request.

### Alternatives considered
- Template interpolation in provider config (#16387): good for identity placeholders, cannot express computed per-call values.
- Rely on `compat.sendSessionAffinityHeaders` (#149615): fixed header set, provider-gated, no plugin input.
- A new standalone hook name: larger surface (registry, metadata, manifest permissions) for the same capability.

### Impact
Affected: plugin authors and self-hosters whose inference gateway routes requests by metadata.
Severity: blocks a supported integration path; today they must fork or patch.
Frequency: every embedded model call in those setups.
Consequence: forks drift, and the workaround (reusing one static header value) produces misleading routing behavior.

### Evidence/examples
- `src/plugins/hook-model.types.ts`: `PluginHookBeforeModelRequestResult` is `{ payload: unknown }`.
- `packages/llm-core/src/types.ts`: `StreamOptions.headers` and the `sendSessionAffinityHeaders` compatibility flag already carry per-request headers to the transport; the capability exists, only the plugin-facing gate is missing.
- `src/plugins/hook-model.ts`: `mergeResults: (_previous, next) => next` means two hooks would overwrite each other's headers; the merge semantics need to be defined as part of this.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?
Yes, I plan to implement this myself

### Additional information
I am happy to scope this down to exactly what you would accept — including dropping it if `sendSessionAffinityHeaders` is meant to be the only supported path. This is specifically about computed values a plugin already has in hand, not a request for template interpolation.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A non-empty `plugins.allow` does not keep out a bundled plugin once its config entry says `plugins.entries.<id>.enabled: true`. The plugin is resolved as enabled ("enabled in config") and the running gateway lists it as enabled, although it is not in `plugins.allow`. It stays enabled for as long as the entry is there, whatever `plugins.allow` says.

The docs read as if the allowlist should still apply: `docs/gateway/config-cloud-workers.md` ("Bundled provider plugins are selected automatically when configured, but explicit disables and `plugins.allow` still apply"), and `docs/plugins/manage-plugins.md` describes enabling as adding the plugin to a restrictive `plugins.allow`, which implies the allowlist is the gate. `resolvePluginActivationDecisionShared` also checks `allow` before honouring an explicit selection (`dist/config-normalization-shared-*.mjs`, the `not-in-allowlist` return), so the override seems to come from somewhere before that check.

### Steps to reproduce

Seen with the bundled `kie` plugin (a video-generation provider, `enabledByDefault: true`); any bundled plugin left out of a non-empty allowlist should do.

1. Gateway config with a non-empty `plugins.allow` that does NOT list `kie` (e.g. a list of other bundled plugin ids), and no `plugins.entries.kie`.
2. `openclaw plugins inspect kie --json` → `"enabled": false`, `"status": "disabled"`, `"activationReason": "not in allowlist"`. `openclaw gateway call plugins.list --json` → `kie` with `"enabled": false`.
3. Edit the config file: set `plugins.entries.kie.enabled` to `true` (hand edit; the gateway hot-reloads plugin config). Leave `plugins.allow` unchanged.
4. `openclaw plugins inspect kie --json` → `"enabled": true`, `"status": "loaded"`, `"activationSource": "explicit"`, `"activationReason": "enabled in config"`. `openclaw gateway call plugins.list --json` → `kie` with `"enabled": true`.
5. Rewrite `plugins.allow` again (still without `kie`): `kie` stays enabled in both views as long as the entry is `true`.

### Expected behavior

`kie` stays disabled with "not in allowlist" while `plugins.allow` is non-empty and does not list it, whatever `plugins.entries.kie.enabled` says. An operator who restricts plugins with `plugins.allow` should not have that undone by a single entry flag. (If entry-enables are meant to win, the docs should say so and `plugins.deny` should be documented as the only hard block.)

### Actual behavior

The entry flag wins over the allowlist: the plugin is resolved as enabled ("enabled in config") and the gateway lists it as enabled.

`plugins.deny` is documented as authoritative ("An explicit `plugins.deny` entry remains authoritative"), so it is the workaround; we have not yet measured it on this version.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.36 (npm, global install)

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64), Node 24

### Install method

npm global

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

The secret-egress proxy builds its upstream TLS trust from `tls.rootCertificates`, so HTTPS origins trusted through the Gateway process's `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` or `--use-system-ca` settings still fail through the proxy.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start the Gateway with `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` pointing to a private CA or self-signed appliance certificate.
2. Enable `secrets.egressProxy.enabled` and bind a protected secret to that HTTPS hostname.
3. Make a Gateway-hosted exec request through the generated proxy environment.
4. Observe the proxy return HTTP 502 while a stock Node HTTPS request in the same startup trust context validates the origin.

A deterministic fixture reproduces this by adding a generated CA to Node's default CA set with `tls.setDefaultCACertificates()`: the proxy fails upstream TLS because `proxy-server.ts` replaces that set with `rootCertificates`.

## Expected behavior

The proxy should preserve the Gateway process's effective Node default CA trust while keeping certificate-chain and hostname verification enabled. Node documents `tls.getCACertificates("default")` as the CA set used by default TLS clients, including startup `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` and optional system CAs.

## Actual behavior

The proxy creates its upstream `HttpsAgent` and subprocess trust bundle from `tls.rootCertificates`, which is only Node's bundled Mozilla store. The upstream request fails with a proxy 502 (`Secret egress proxy could not reach the upstream host`) for an otherwise trusted private HTTPS origin.

## OpenClaw version

2026.8.1 and current `main` at `228ccdf6fd08a1e3e5c6612bd2ff9bd22c8c4eea`

## Operating system

Linux 7.0.0-30-generic x64; Node.js 22.23.2

## Install method

npm global for the live reproduction; pnpm source checkout for the regression fixture

## Model

N/A (Gateway-hosted exec TLS path)

## Provider / routing chain

Gateway-hosted exec -> authenticated loopback secret-egress proxy -> local HTTPS origin

## Additional provider/model setup details

The protected sentinel remains exact-host destination-bound. The failure occurs during the proxy's verified upstream TLS handshake, before the origin receives a request.

## Logs

```shell
pre-fix fixture: expected HTTP 200, received HTTP 502
body: Secret egress proxy could not reach the upstream host.
direct Node path: DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT without startup trust; succeeds when the same certificate is in Node's default CA set
```

## Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

A local patch replacing `rootCertificates` with `getCACertificates("default")` makes the new regression pass, preserves all existing secret-egress tests, and successfully completes a credential-free live request through the patched proxy to a self-signed local HTTPS appliance with status 200. The generated subprocess trust bundle also contains the added default CA.

Focused validation:

- pre-fix: 1 failed / 20 passed (`proxy-server.test.ts`)
- post-fix: 29 passed across `proxy-server.test.ts` and `proxy-server.lifecycle.test.ts`
- live credential-free patched-proxy TLS proof: HTTP 200, exact expected host, no substitution

## Impact and severity

- Affected: operators using protected secret destination binding with private-CA or self-signed local HTTPS services.
- Severity: workflow blocker; disabling TLS verification is not an acceptable workaround, and `bypassHosts` cannot substitute protected sentinels.
- Frequency: deterministic for every request to an origin trusted only outside Node's bundled roots.
- Consequence: protected local API integrations cannot be used despite valid Gateway startup trust configuration.

## Additional information

The smallest repair is to snapshot `tls.getCACertificates("default")` when the Gateway starts the secret-egress proxy, then use that set plus the proxy CA for both the upstream `HttpsAgent` and generated subprocess trust bundle. This adds no new config surface and keeps TLS chain and hostname verification enabled. The affected source and documentation paths are secops-owned by CODEOWNERS; a reviewed local patch and regression are ready for owner involvement.

### Summary
On `OpenClaw 2026.11.10 (6ea542f)` (Linux x64, Node v26.12.1), running `openclaw infer model run --agent <id> --model "<provider>/<model>@<profile>"` via the Gateway fails with `modelPolicy.allow` rejection even when `<provider>/<model>` is explicitly allowed in `agents.defaults.modelPolicy.allow`.

Meanwhile:
- `openclaw infer model run --agent <id> --model "<provider>/<model>"` (without `@<profile>`) succeeds on the Gateway transport.
- Cron jobs configured with `<provider>/<model>@<profile>` also succeed on the same Gateway.
- `openclaw infer model run --local` is now rejected while the Gateway owns the state root (`requires exclusive offline state ownership. Omit --local to run it through the Gateway`), leaving no way for a CLI caller to target an explicit auth profile when `agents.defaults.modelPolicy.allow` enumerates explicit models instead of `<provider>/*`.

### Reproduction
1. Configure an agent with explicit models in `agents.defaults.modelPolicy.allow`, e.g. `["anthropic/claude-opus-5-5"]`, and multiple Anthropic auth profiles (e.g. `anthropic:a`, `anthropic:b`).
2. Start the Gateway on `2026.11.10`.
3. Run:
   ```bash
   openclaw infer model run --agent main --model "anthropic/claude-opus-5-5@anthropic:a" --prompt "Reply with ok" --json
   ```

### Observed result
```text
Gateway owning ~/.openclaw on local port 18789 could not complete agent for agent model credentials:
Model override "anthropic/claude-opus-5-5@anthropic:a" is not allowed for agent "main" by agents.defaults.modelPolicy.allow.
Add "anthropic/claude-opus-5-5@anthropic:a" or "anthropic/*" to agents.defaults.modelPolicy.allow, or remove/empty the list to allow any model.
```

Running the same command without `@anthropic:a` succeeds (`"ok": true, "transport": "gateway"`).

### Root cause in `2026.11.10`
In `dist/agent-command-*.mjs` (`resolveEmbeddedModelSelection`), the explicit override path parses `d` with `parseAgentCommandModelRef(...)` without stripping a trailing `@<profile>` via `splitTrailingAuthProfile(...)` before checking `p.allows(n)`. As a result, `n.model` retains `@<profile>` and fails exact allowlist matching against `<provider>/<model>`.

### Expected result
`resolveEmbeddedModelSelection` (or `parseAgentCommandModelRef`) should split any trailing `@<profile>` auth-profile specifier before evaluating `agents.defaults.modelPolicy.allow` (matching how cron job model overrides handle `<provider>/<model>@<profile>`).

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

When a scheduled automation fails because the Codex harness hit a ChatGPT usage limit, the failure notice usually says `Cause: unknown`. Only some runs get `Cause: rate_limit`. Runs that fail afterwards, while the auth profile is in cooldown, also say `Cause: unknown`. The provider error class is known at each of these points but doesn't reach `errorReason`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On 2026.11.10, use the Codex harness (ChatGPT sign-in) with several isolated cron jobs scheduled at the same minute.
2. Exhaust the account's Codex usage window.
3. Read the run history (`openclaw cron runs --all --json`) and the failure notices.

### Expected behavior

Every run that failed because of the usage limit records `errorReason: "rate_limit"`, and its notice says `Cause: rate_limit`. That covers the cooldown runs that follow, too.

### Actual behavior

Run history from one gateway, all within the same few minutes:

| Run error (start) | `errorReason` |
|---|---|
| `Codex reported a usage or quota limit. You’ve hit your usage limit…` | `rate_limit` |
| `cron isolated run failed: Codex reported a usage or quota limit. You’ve hit your usage limit…` | `unknown` |
| `Prepared auth profiles are temporarily unavailable for openai/gpt-6.2-sol.` (the next 20–30 minutes of runs) | `unknown` |

So the notice for the second and third kinds reads `Automation "…" failed N times` followed by `Cause: unknown`, which hides the real cause and its fix (wait for the reset or switch accounts). Running `resolveFailoverReasonFromError` on the second message returns `rate_limit`. The classifier recognizes it, but these paths never call it.

### Where the class is dropped

- `src/cron/isolated-agent/run.ts`: when the run finalizes with a run-level `meta.error` (rendered as `cron isolated run failed: …` by `formatCronRunLevelError`), it calls `resolveCronAgentErrorClassification(terminalOutcome)` with no reason, so `failed` becomes `unknown`. The thrown path only recovers a reason from a `FailoverError` instance.
- `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/runtime-preparation.ts`: harness-owned auth throws a plain `Error("Prepared auth profiles are temporarily unavailable …")` when every prepared profile is in cooldown. `resolveProfilesUnavailableReason` (or the cooldown probe policy's `unavailableReason`) already knows the cooldown came from `rate_limit`, but it isn't attached.

The comment on `resolveCronAgentErrorClassification` rules out display text driving retries. A fix that carries the producer's typed reason (a `FailoverError` from the Codex usage-limit error and from the cooldown refusal, or a reason field on `meta.error`) would keep retry policy unchanged and still let the notice name the cause.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.10

### Operating system

Amazon Linux 2023 (aarch64)

### Install method

npm global

### Model

openai/gpt-6.2-sol

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw cron (isolated agentTurn) -> codex plugin (app-server) -> ChatGPT Codex Responses

### Impact and severity

Operators receiving the notice can't tell a usage-limit outage from a broken job. In our case several gateways showed `Cause: unknown` during a usage-limit outage and the cause had to be recovered from run history by hand.

### Bug type

### Beta release blocker

### Summary

After updating from 2026.10.10 to 2026.11.3, delegated child work can receive the task and produce a handoff, but the parent cannot independently verify delivery receipt or ACK correlation.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure a parent agent `tech` with `system-tester` in its subagent allowlist.
2. Delegate one read-only task with a unique task_id.
3. Observe the parent/child lifecycle and completion.
4. Repeat after upgrading OpenClaw from 2026.10.10 to 2026.11.3.

### Expected behavior

The parent should receive a completion event with independently verifiable delivery receipt and an ACK correlated to the exact task_id, followed by a valid handoff/result.

### Actual behavior

The child receives the correct task_id and can produce a valid 9-field handoff JSON, but no separate delivery receipt or ACK containing/correlating the exact task_id is observable. Probe r5 remains blocked. `accepted`, `queued`, and `done` are not treated as receipt or ACK.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.3 (847611d); regression observed from 2026.10.10

### Operating system

Windows 11, Windows_NT 10.0.26200 (x64)

### Install method

npm package / installed runtime

### Model

shop/openclaw

### Provider / routing chain

## Summary
Since 2026.10.9 the Control UI no longer starts on iPadOS 17.7.x (Safari 17, and Chrome on iPad, same WebKit). The page shows the recovery panel "Control UI did not start". It worked on the previous release. Private window, cleared site data and no content blockers give the same result.

The device cannot upgrade: iPad Pro 10.5-inch (2017) tops out at iPadOS 17, which still receives Apple security updates.

## Likely cause
The startup chunks call APIs Safari 17 does not have, without a feature check:
- `URL.parse(...)` (Safari 18.0+): `ui-*.js` (3 calls) and `control-ui-core-*.js` (11 calls) in `dist/control-ui/assets/`

Other newer APIs we found (`Uint8Array.fromHex`, `toHex`) are already guarded.

Not confirmed with a device console. Shimming `URL.parse` and the Iterator helper methods in a script injected before the module entry passes local tests with the natives removed.

## Request
I saw #168360 (dormant browser-capability screen, iOS/Safari 26.2 floor at the Solid cutover). Until that cutover the documented requirements have not changed, so either:
1. guard these calls (`new URL()` in try/catch instead of `URL.parse`, `Array.from(map.entries()).map(...)`), or
2. ship the capability screen now, so Safari 17 users get a clear "unsupported browser" message instead of a crash and retry loop.

## Environment
- OpenClaw 2026.10.9 (8b18b55), gateway on macOS 27.0.1, Control UI over Tailscale Serve
- Client: iPadOS 17.7.8 (also on 17.7.11), Safari 17 and Chrome for iOS

issues.body:
Version: 2026.11.10 (6ea542f), Linux, managed `openclaw` profile (local CDP, Playwright).

What happens: `browser` action `open` with `label: "x"` sometimes returns `{targetId, title: "", url: <requested url>, type: "page"}` with no `tabId`, `suggestedTargetId` or `label`. A later call with `targetId: "x"` fails "tab not found: browser tab \"x\" not found". `tabs` lists the tab (same raw targetId) with a fresh `tabId` and no label. Seen several times a day on facebook.com Marketplace pages (which redirect after load).

Expected: the label is assigned whenever `open` succeeds (docs/cli/browser.md: "Assign a label with `open --label`"), or `open` reports that it could not assign it.

Cause (dist/server-context-*.mjs, openTab): after createTargetViaCdp, OpenClaw polls the tab list for OPEN_TAB_DISCOVERY_WINDOW_MS (2000 ms) and only calls adoptOwnedTab/assignTabAlias (which sets the label) when the tab shows up. Otherwise it returns `withTabOwnership({targetId, title: "", url, type: "page"})` without assignTabAlias, so the label is dropped. The /json/new path also returns the tab unlabelled when the committed navigation URL is unknown (`return S ? adoptValidatedTab(C, …) : C`).

Suggested fix: assign the tab alias (tabId + label) by targetId in the fallback branches too, or retry the lookup on the next tab listing, and return `tabId`/`label` consistently.

Workaround: `tabs`, find the entry with the targetId `open` returned, `openclaw browser tab label <tabId> <label>`.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

With the Codex harness on its managed (bundled) app-server, warm model requests in a turn stop reusing the prompt cache for their last several thousand tokens. Running the **same bundled binary** through `plugins.entries.codex.config.appServer.command` brings warm reuse back to about 99%. The managed launch owns the parent-local inference relay (`ownCodexInferenceClient`); an explicit command does not. The size of the lost tail tracks the size of the skills, persona and memory text, which the relay adds to each request's `instructions` in `inference-context.ts` `prepare()` rather than keeping it in the native thread's developer instructions.

### Steps to reproduce

1. OpenClaw 2026.11.10 with `@openclaw/codex` 2026.11.10 (bundled `@openai/codex` 0.172.0) and ChatGPT sign-in on `openai/gpt-6.2-sol`. Use a workspace with a typical skills catalog (a few thousand tokens of skill descriptions).
2. Leave `plugins.entries.codex.config.appServer.command` unset, so the managed binary runs.
3. Run a nondelivered turn that makes five sequential read-only tool calls (`openclaw agent --session-key agent:main:cache-a --message "Run date -u; uptime; ls ~ | head -5; df -h / | tail -1; whoami as five separate tool calls, then reply DONE."`).
4. Read `last_token_usage` (`input_tokens` / `cached_input_tokens`) from each `token_count` event in that thread's Codex rollout.
5. Set `appServer.command` to the bundled binary's own path (`.../node_modules/@openai/codex-linux-arm64/vendor/aarch64-unknown-linux-musl/bin/codex`), wait for the hot reload, and repeat with a new session key.

### Expected behavior

Each warm request reuses the previous request's whole input, as with the explicit command: cached ≈ previous request's input.

### Actual behavior

Measured on the same host and account, a few minutes apart (input/cached per request):

| Launch | Requests (input/cached) | Warm hit |
|---|---|---|
| Managed, run 1 | 36597/18304 36692/31360 36811/31360 36926/31360 37038/31360 37120/31360 | 84.9% |
| Managed, run 2 | 36597/0 36709/31360 36827/31360 36941/31360 37053/0 37134/31360 | 67.9% |
| Same binary via `appServer.command` | 36160/0 36272/35968 36390/36096 36507/36096 36618/36352 36700/36352 | 99.1% |
| Same, repeated twice more | identical pattern | 99.1%, 99.1% |

Codex 0.169.1 and 0.170.0 through `appServer.command` also give 99.0%, so the Codex version is not the variable.

On three busier production gateways, the managed launch has lost a constant amount per request since the switch: each warm request's cached count is the previous request's input minus about 7k tokens on one gateway and about 10.5k or 26k on another (two workloads with larger skills and persona text), against near 0 before. Daily cache hit fell from 91–95% to 74–82%, and uncached input roughly tripled, which drains ChatGPT plan limits fast.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.10

### Operating system

Amazon Linux 2023 (aarch64)

### Install method

npm global

### Model

openai/gpt-6.2-sol

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> codex plugin (managed app-server, stdio) -> parent-local inference relay -> ChatGPT Codex Responses (WebSocket)

### Additional provider/model setup details

`plugins.entries.codex.config.codexDynamicToolsLoading: "searchable"`. No proxy or custom CA (so `supportsInferenceEnvironment` admits the relay).

### Impact and severity

Every turn with more than one model request pays uncached input for its skills, persona and memory text on every request. On ChatGPT plans this exhausted a weekly Codex limit in under four days. Workaround: set `appServer.command` explicitly (we point it at a mise-installed Codex of the bundled version), which leaves the relay off.

### Additional information

Relevant code: `extensions/codex/src/app-server/inference-context.ts` `prepare()` appends `registration.text` to `instructions` on every turn request; `thread-lifecycle-run.ts` clears `refreshableInstructions` from native thread state whenever `params.inferenceRoute` is set. We have not captured the relay's outgoing request bodies, so where the backend places that per-request `instructions` text in the prompt is an inference from the usage pattern.

issues.body:
## Problem

OpenClaw sends operational metadata to models even when it is not useful for the current task. Host, session, workspace, OS, Node and repeated sender identifiers consume context; mixing invariant channel policy with changing per-turn facts also risks needless cache invalidation. This is especially visible on local models, but the design principle applies to all providers.

## Proposed improvement

Project only the runtime facts the model needs for its effective capabilities; keep transport and operational metadata host-side where possible. Separate stable policy from transient conversation facts, and deduplicate sender metadata only when identity and attribution remain unambiguous. Preserve chronology, mention/reply semantics, trust boundaries, tool requirements and checkpoint compatibility. Do not globally remove tool instructions or security policy.

## Evidence

A version-pinned operator overlay on OpenClaw 2026.11.10, Windows, local Gemma via openai-completions, tool-free Discord, reduced one runtime block from 405 to 57 characters (85.9%) on consecutive actual model inputs. Follow-up recall checks succeeded. The observed first-token times for three subsequent requests were approximately 97, 5 and 40 seconds; total inference times were approximately 118, 15 and 55 seconds. These are not controlled speed benchmarks: cache behavior, changing history and prior runaway generations confound the timings. No cross-provider correctness or performance claim is made.

[Our public proof-of-concept write-up and optimization roadmap](https://github.com/Animeleague/openclaw/blob/bank/prompt-optimisation-v3.1-2026-11-27/live-bank/2026-11-27-prompt-optimisation-v3.1/README.md). This is a scoped runtime-overlay experiment, not a published native plugin. The executable recovery materials are not included in the public branch because the original fixtures contain private deployment details.

Related cache investigation: #202001. This proposal focuses on reducing redundant model-facing data and keeping stable policy separate, rather than claiming to resolve every cache invalidation cause.

## Scope and limitations

The proof of concept is tied to exact compiled bundles. An upstream implementation needs current source inspection, capability-aware projection, regression tests for identity/trust boundaries, checkpoint transitions and representative tool-enabled routes, plus controlled benchmarks. Our fork has diverged from upstream; any proposed change should be isolated on a clean upstream-based branch rather than importing unrelated fork commits. No runtime behavior changes are proposed for merge without these checks.

We would welcome maintainer guidance on the appropriate source-level extension point.

## Working plugin: transient turn context

[OpenClaw Transient Turn Context v0.1 (source, tests and measured results)](https://github.com/Animeleague/openclaw/tree/bank/transient-turn-context-v0.1-2026-11-27/live-bank/2026-11-27-transient-turn-context-v0.1) is a complementary, live-demonstrated proof of concept using the existing provider buildReplayPolicy hook. It sets appendOnlyRuntimeContext to false for the tested local route, so the existing inference-boundary filter retains the current typed runtime-context carrier rather than replaying every historical snapshot. No transcript deletion or core patch is required.

On the tested route, historical carriers fell from 6–9 to 1, input tokens from 14,805 to 6,381 (56.9% reduction), and mean short-exchange input growth from 1,080 to 211 tokens (80.5% reduction). Recent room recall passed. Derived warm-cache reuse fell from 92.0% to 82.2%; mean fresh tokens rose from 1,092 to 1,216, so this is a context-capacity improvement, not proof of improved warm latency. This is distinct from the subsequent V3.1 metadata compaction. The generic renamed package is locally tested but has not itself been installed live; other providers and rollback still require validation.

## What happens

I reproduced this on main `288e52aab044fc885aa8b4ed47d59a46f08e3da7` using the repository CrabBox wrapper on AWS, a real Gateway, and a live OpenAI Responses model on the embedded runtime.

A parent receives `status: accepted` from `sessions_spawn` with `context: fork`, but the child's model input contains `aborted` for the same tool-call ID. Both captured forks showed the contradiction. Both children completed in this small sample, so I did not independently reproduce task abandonment.

## Reproduction

1. Give the parent a unique context marker.
2. Write a different marker to a file without including its value in the prompt.
3. Ask the parent to fork one child that reads the file and returns both markers.
4. Capture the Responses requests and compare the parent's spawn receipt with the inherited result for that same call ID in the child.

## Expected

A result absent at the fork boundary must not be presented as an aborted operation. Preserve the inherited context and completed tool results without changing the parent's transcript.

## Cause

The fork copies the in-flight spawn call before its result is available. Responses history repair fills the missing result with `aborted`.

## Verification limits

The wire contradiction was observed in 2/2 forks. The unchanged-main live fixture also reported `Native worker execution owners have not joined` during Gateway shutdown after collecting the results.

issues.body:
### Bug type
Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker
No

### Summary
Running `openclaw channels add` to update an existing A2A peer's inbound token removes that peer's independently configured `url` and `outboundToken`. The command reports success, but the saved peer can no longer receive outbound messages.

### Steps to reproduce
1. In a disposable profile, configure an A2A peer with an inbound token and outbound settings:
   ```json
   {"channels":{"a2a":{"enabled":true,"peers":{"partner":{"token":"fixture-old-inbound","url":"https://peer.example.test/a2a/v1","outboundToken":"fixture-outbound"}}}}}
   ```
2. Run `openclaw --profile <disposable-profile> channels add --channel a2a --peer-name partner --peer-token fixture-new-inbound`.
3. Inspect `channels.a2a.peers.partner` in that profile's saved configuration.

### Expected behavior
The peer keeps its URL and outbound credential while its inbound token changes to `fixture-new-inbound`.

### Actual behavior
The command exits successfully and the peer becomes:
```json
{"token":"fixture-new-inbound"}
```
Both outbound fields are removed. An unrelated peer in the same configuration is preserved.

### OpenClaw version
Source commit `e741fd0d21ff7f9857a9c49f91d95166beaae83f`; the affected setup owner was also checked against current main before reporting.

### Operating system
macOS 27.0.1 arm64, Node 26.12.1.

### Install method
Source checkout with frozen dependencies.

### Model
Not applicable; the configuration command requires no inference.

### Provider / routing chain
A2A channel setup → saved peer configuration → outbound A2A delivery.

### Logs
Reproduced with the real source CLI in a separate named profile, synthetic credentials and a temporary configuration:
```text
command exit: 0
before token: fixture-old-inbound
before url: https://peer.example.test/a2a/v1
before outboundToken: fixture-outbound
after:  token=fixture-new-inbound
other peer preserved: true
```

### Impact and severity
Updating an inbound credential breaks a previously configured outbound peer until its URL and outbound credential are restored. The [documented outbound configuration](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/e741fd0d21ff7f9857a9c49f91d95166beaae83f/docs/channels/a2a.md#configure-outbound-peers) treats these as separate settings; a peer without a URL cannot receive outbound messages.

### Additional information
The [setup adapter](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/e741fd0d21ff7f9857a9c49f91d95166beaae83f/extensions/a2a/src/channel-base.ts) preserves the peer map but replaces the selected peer object with `{ token: peerToken }`. Updating an existing peer should retain its other authored fields, including unresolved outbound credential references. Adding a new peer should continue to work as before.

issues.body:
### Summary

Introduce an open, backend-neutral Memory Reliability Contract (MRC) defining minimum reliability guarantees and a shared conformance test suite for OpenClaw memory providers.

The goal is not to create another memory engine or require everyone to use the same database. It is to establish a trustworthy foundation that different implementations can build upon.

Different engines. Different algorithms. One common foundation of reliability.

### Problem to solve

The AI agent ecosystem has many memory implementations, including OpenClaw Memory Core, Mem0, Mnemosyne, and others. They compete on retrieval, consolidation, storage architecture, and performance.

That diversity is valuable. However, users still encounter basic reliability problems:

* An agent claims to have saved information without actually performing a write.
* Information exists in persistent storage, but the agent incorrectly claims it is missing.
* Repeated information creates duplicates.
* Corrections leave conflicting or outdated facts behind.
* Automatic summarization or consolidation can distort original information.
* Users cannot easily audit, restore, or migrate their memories between systems.

These are not merely differences in algorithms. They undermine fundamental expectations of persistent memory.

The missing piece is a common reliability contract, independent of the memory implementation.

### Proposed solution

Establish a minimal Memory Reliability Contract (MRC) with eight core principles.

The contract should define observable guarantees and operational semantics, without prescribing databases, embedding models, search algorithms, or consolidation strategies.

1. Verified writes

A memory operation must not be reported as successfully committed unless the storage layer confirms its completion.

A model’s intention to save information is not proof that the operation occurred.

2. Information integrity

Original user-provided information must not be silently altered.

Source statements should remain distinguishable from model-generated summaries, interpretations, and inferred facts.

3. Duplicate control

Repeated identical operations must not create unnecessary duplicate records.

Semantic duplicates may require probabilistic detection, but uncertain matches should be handled explicitly rather than silently merged.

4. Controlled updates and conflicts

Corrections must have defined update semantics.

Conflicting information should be detected and handled according to an explicit policy rather than silently appended or overwritten.

5. Provenance

Memory records should support stable identifiers, source attribution, creation timestamps, and modification history.

6. Auditability and recovery

Memory changes must be inspectable. The system should provide a way to detect failed or incorrect operations and restore previous states where supported.

7. Enforced permissions

Read, create, update, and delete permissions must be enforced by the runtime or storage interface, not solely by natural-language instructions.

8. Portability

Memory systems should support documented export and import of original information, identifiers, provenance, and relevant history without silently discarding data.

⸻

Implementation approach

The contract should separate three responsibilities:

* Language model: interprets user intent and proposes memory operations.
* Memory provider: validates, executes, and returns verifiable operation results.
* Agent runtime: exposes the actual operation status and must not treat an unexecuted or failed operation as a confirmed write.

The proposal does not require perfect natural-language understanding. Where semantic certainty is impossible, the system should preserve the original information and explicitly represent uncertainty.

Shared conformance tests

Provide a reusable test suite covering:

1. Successful write with verifiable confirmation.
2. Repeated identical write without duplication.
3. Update with version/history preservation.
4. Conflicting information and ambiguity handling.
5. Retrieval after restarting the agent.
6. Failed writes and missing retrieval results.
7. Unauthorized operations being rejected.
8. Export/import round-trip integrity.

Multilingual retrieval, semantic deduplication, and consolidation quality should be evaluated separately through measurable benchmarks rather than represented as absolute guarantees.

A practical first milestone could be a written specification and a backend-neutral test harness, initially available as an optional conformance suite for memory plugins.

Existing memory providers should be able to adopt the contract incrementally, without requiring a rewrite of their implementations.

### Alternatives considered

Prompt-only rules: Insufficient. Language models can omit tool calls, falsely claim completion, or misinterpret instructions.

Mandating one memory engine: Would limit experimentation and create unnecessary dependence on a single implementation.

Building another memory plugin: Does not solve the underlying interoperability and reliability problem.

Standardizing every algorithm: Unnecessary. Search, consolidation, embeddings, and storage strategies should remain implementation choices.

The proposed contract focuses on common observable guarantees rather than a specific implementation.

### Impact

Affected users: OpenClaw users relying on persistent memory, developers of memory plugins, and other agent frameworks that may adopt the contract.

Severity: High for trust and data integrity when silent errors occur. Some issues are intermittent and model-dependent.

Consequences:

* Lost or distorted information.
* Manual verification of memory operations.
* Inconsistent behavior across sessions.
* Difficulty switching memory backends.
* Reduced confidence in autonomous agents.

A shared contract could improve interoperability and make reliability claims independently testable without forcing all providers into the same architecture.

This proposal is intended as a foundation for future reliability improvements rather than an immediate replacement of existing memory systems.

### Evidence/examples

During local testing with OpenClaw 2026.11.5 and a locally hosted language model, two distinct failures were observed.

Case A — False write confirmation

A user explicitly requested that information be remembered.

The agent stated that it had saved the information. However, inspection of the session’s tool-call history showed that no write operation occurred.

The information had not been persisted.

Case B — Existing information not retrieved

Information was successfully stored in Markdown memory files and indexed.

In another session, the agent repeatedly stated that the information was unavailable.

It eventually retrieved the information only after an explicit request to inspect the relevant file.

These examples demonstrate different failure classes:

* Unverified write acknowledgements.
* Unreliable retrieval of existing persistent information.

They do not establish that every memory backend has the same defect. They illustrate why a common reliability contract should distinguish storage guarantees from semantic retrieval quality.

Related discussions

* [#70049 — Canonical semantic memory writes](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/70049)
* [#60572 — Multi-slot memory architecture](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/60572)
* [OpenClaw VISION.md](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/VISION.md) — discusses introducing shared contracts when multiple independent implementations address the same capability.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, I am not planning to implement this myself.

### Additional information

This is a request for a shared interface contract and a testable foundation, not an immediate rewrite of OpenClaw’s memory system.

Existing plugins should be able to adopt the specification incrementally. An initial version could distinguish mandatory storage-level guarantees from optional semantic-quality benchmarks.

The specification should ideally remain independent of OpenClaw so that other agent frameworks and memory providers can adopt it.

The purpose is not to stop innovation or reduce the number of memory engines.

It is to establish a small set of fundamental guarantees that all implementations can share.

Different engines. Different algorithms. One common foundation of reliability.

A system should be free to innovate above that foundation, but users should not have to question whether a confirmed memory operation actually happened.

issues.body:
### Bug type
Regression / update blocker

### Summary
`openclaw update --yes --json` from 2026.11.9 → 2026.11.10 (macOS arm64, npm global install, SQLite state ~1.3 GiB, 5 agent databases at schema 38) fails in `validating` → `candidate-doctor`:

```
Failed: candidate-doctor — Exit code: 1
Failing check plugin-doctor-post-session-state (blocked-by-session-repair-failure):
  Post-session plugin repair was blocked because prerequisite session repair failed:
  Error: cannot read legacy session store [redacted-path]
Failing check update (doctor-failed)
Doctor stopped because a state migration refused to continue.
```

The updater rolls back cleanly: the gateway keeps running on 2026.11.9 and never stops.

The throw is `onUnreadable` in `migrateLegacyMainSessionKeysInternal` (`legacy-main-session-migration-*.mjs`). In `doctor-fix` mode any store that `readClaimsFromStores` can't read aborts the whole Doctor, and the diagnostics redact the only identifying detail (the store path and the underlying error), so the operator can't tell which store it was.

### Relevant candidate-doctor stderr just before the failure (sanitized)
```
[state/agent-db] agent database integrity gate for <agent-A>: reason=no-proof, mode=deferred, outcome=pending
[state/agent-db] agent database clean-close receipt: verification-missing; agent=<agent-A>
Session recovery warning: ... Retired terminal unmatched legacy restart custody (original state backed up).   (x2)
Session SQLite: Canonicalized entry state for 2 durable session row(s).
```
`<agent-A>` is the default (sole configured) agent, the only agent DB without a `.seal` sidecar, and the one with live WAL. Also present: a stray pre-migration state root nested inside that agent's dir (`agents/<agent-A>/agent/state/openclaw.sqlite`, user_version 17, plus `agents/<agent-A>/agent/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite`) from an old run. Either could be the "unreadable" store. The 2026.11.9 `doctor --lint --all` reports no session-store findings.

### Expected
- Either skip or preserve unreadable or held stores (as `selectSessionStoreMaintenanceTargets` already does for held stores, cf. #172259), or report the failing store path and error class unredacted in the update report so it can be fixed.
- `doctor --lint` on the installed version should be able to surface the same finding before an update attempt.

### Related
#172259 (closed; same family: the legacy-main scan opens DBs that the earlier repair skipped).

### Environment
2026.11.9 (0032b1d) → 2026.11.10, macOS 27.0.1 arm64, node 26.12.1, npm global install, stable channel.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In a Telegram direct chat with the default `steer` queue, message A starts a run. While the run is in its tool calls, message B is steered into it. The agent answers B with `message(action=send)` without `final`. OpenClaw treats that send as final and ends the whole run. A gets no answer and no failure notice.

The docs say two things here. `docs/concepts/agent-loop.md` says a confirmed final send to the current source conversation ends the run loop, and the tool's `final` description says an omitted `final` means a completed send. But `docs/concepts/messages.md` also says: "A final source reply completes only the input it answers." Here the reply completes B, and it also silently ends the work for A.

Related: #193481 and #127139 report the same mechanism (a send without `final` ends the turn) in a run with a single input. The automated review on #193481 calls that behavior deliberate and documented and asks for a maintainer decision. This report is about a run with two committed inputs, where the documented contract says the reply completes only one of them. #197333 is a different cause: GPT-5/6 models choose to answer only the newest steered message. Here the model (Claude) said it would answer B and then finish A, and the run ended after the send.

### Steps to reproduce

This was seen twice in one hour in production. I have not reproduced it on demand, because step 4 depends on the model's choice.

1. Run OpenClaw 2026.11.2 with a Telegram direct chat, the built-in (`openclaw`) runtime and an Anthropic model. Leave `messages.queue` and `messages.visibleReplies` unset (`steer`, `automatic`).
2. Send message A, a task that needs several tool calls.
3. While the run is in its tool calls, send message B, an unrelated short request. It is steered into the running turn.
4. The agent answers B first with `message(action=send)` to the current chat and no `final` field.

### Expected behavior

The send completes only B. The run continues so A gets its answer, or A gets a visible failure.

### Actual behavior

- B's answer is delivered (`ok: true`, `sourceReplyRoute: "current-source"`). The send had no `replyTo` the first time and `replyTo` set to B the second time.
- The run ends at once: within about 0.1 s of the `message` tool result, the trajectory shows `model.completed`, `trace.artifacts` (`finalStatus: "success"`, `stopReason: "toolUse"`) and `session.ended` (`status: "success"`, `stopReason: "toolUse"`). There is no further model call.
- A gets no reply and no failure message. In the second case the agent had already done A's work but never sent A's result.

Both times the user had to ask again.

### Source

At tag `v2026.11.2` (b556fdf457b0):

- `src/agents/embedded-agent-message-tool-source-reply.ts` L20-22: `resolveMessageToolSourceReplyFinal` returns true when `final` is omitted.
- `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/message-tool-terminal.ts` L104-154: one `finalSourceReplyDelivered` flag shared by all inputs of the run (reset after each tool turn), and `delivered && final` returns `terminate: true` (L154). Nothing checks whether another committed input of the run is still unanswered.

At `main` (9159d33262bf), from reading the source only (not reproduced):

- `message-tool-terminal.ts` L104-188 records final replies per input scope and passes the current input's scope to the `complete` method of the object that `createSourceReplyBatchCompletion` returns (`src/agents/tool-source-reply-completion.ts`). That function's comment says "Final delivery completes only its settled batch, never an unrelated later input". That protects a later input from an earlier input's reply. The reverse case looks unchanged: a final reply for the current input (B) completes the turn, and `(delivered && final)` still returns `terminate: true` (L184-186). Nothing I found checks an earlier input (A) of the same run.

### Suggested fix direction

One of these:

- Do not end the run on a final source reply while another committed input of the same run has no delivered reply.
- Or treat an omitted `final` as `false` once steering has added an input to the running turn.
- At minimum, send a visible failure for the unanswered input instead of ending silently.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.2 (b556fdf457b0), built from source at that tag with 6 local patches. None of them changes `message-tool-terminal.ts`, `embedded-agent-message-tool-source-reply.ts` or steering.

### Operating system

Linux (container on the official `ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.11.2` base image, Kubernetes)

### Install method

Docker image built from source

### Model

anthropic/claude-opus-5-5

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw → Anthropic provider

### Additional provider/model setup details

SSH sandbox backend.

### Logs

Trajectory for one affected run, with IDs and content removed:

```
prompt.submitted   [media attached …] <message A>
tool.call          exec …            (reading files for A)
                   <message B steered into the run>
tool.call          exec …            (work for B)
tool.call          message {"action":"send","message":"<answer to B>"}     # no "final"
tool.result        message {"ok":true,"messageId":"…","sourceReplyRoute":"current-source"}
model.completed    aborted=false
trace.artifacts    finalStatus=success stopReason=toolUse
session.ended      status=success stopReason=toolUse
```

There is no assistant event after the `message` result, and nothing is sent for A.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Impact and severity

Medium. When the agent answers a steered message with a send that omits `final`, the request that started the run is silently dropped with no error.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

after upgrade from 2026.10.10 to 2026.11.2, After a few minutes of normal use or idle time, the Control UI page enters a busy loop. The page's own JavaScript repeatedly calls `Element.getAnimations()`, and each call forces a full style recalculation. One renderer core sits at 100% or more, and the UI stops responding to clicks and typing. The window can still be moved. Quitting and reopening the app clears it.

It happens in two different engines at the same time, the macOS app's WebKit WebContent process and a Microsoft Edge renderer, so it looks like a problem in the Control UI page code and not in one browser.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.11.2 (gateway, CLI and macOS app all on the same release)
- macOS 27.0.1, MacBook Pro (Mac14,6, Apple M2 Max, 32 GB)
- Gateway running locally as the app-managed service, Control UI loaded from it
- Also seen in Microsoft Edge 152 against the same gateway
- Custom theme plugin enabled (the same plugin on a second gateway, running on mac mini, same version 2026.11.2, does not show the problem)

## Observed

- The hot process is the WebKit WebContent process hosting the Control UI (about 100% of one core, around 600 MB resident). A Chromium renderer for a tab on the same gateway shows the same pattern.
- The gateway process stays quiet (roughly 10% CPU) while this happens.
- System load stays low (about 18%), but WindowServer rises to roughly 50% CPU while the loop runs.
- A second gateway on the same release, used from the same app, does not show the problem.

## Stack (WebKit `sample`, main thread, 1,423 of 1,423 samples)

```
WebCore::Page::updateRendering()
  WebCore::AnimationTimelinesController::updateAnimationsAndSendEvents()
    JSC microtask checkpoint
      page JavaScript (microtask)
        WebCore::jsElementPrototypeFunction_getAnimations
          WebCore::Element::getAnimations()
            WebCore::Document::updateStyleIfNeeded()
              Style::TreeResolver::resolve()
                Style::TreeResolver::resolveComposedTree()
                  resetStyleForNonRenderedDescendants()
                    Node::isComposedTreeDescendantOf()
```

All time is in style resolution reached from `getAnimations()` inside a microtask during the rendering update. No other thread is busy.

## Suspected code

`dist/control-ui/assets/control-ui-boot-shared-Ihze6w_j.js` contains an overlay controller that polls animations on an element and reschedules itself while any are still running:

```js
function oe(){return a.getAnimations().filter(...)}
function ce(){return oe().length>0}
function le(e,t){
  ... requestAnimationFrame(()=>{
    ... Promise.allSettled(oe().map(e=>e.finished)).then(()=>{
      ... if(!i.isOpen(a)&&ce()){le(!1,t);return} ...
```

If an animation on that element never finishes or is replaced on each pass (for example, a looping or infinite animation, or one restarted by the theme), the condition `!isOpen && ce()` stays true. `le` then schedules itself again from a resolved promise on every frame. Each pass calls `getAnimations()`, which forces style recalculation. That matches the stack above. I did not run the page under a debugger, so this is the most likely loop and not a confirmed one.

## Expected

An idle Control UI should use no CPU. A loop that waits on animations should be bounded, or should stop when the element is hidden or the animation is infinite.

## Workaround

Quit and reopen the app.

## Not the cause (checked)

- Reduce Motion is off, so that setting does not explain it.
- The gateway is not busy, and its log shows nothing unusual during the spin.
- Page load alone does not trigger it. A normal load peaks briefly at about 84% CPU and then settles to idle.

### Steps to reproduce

The freeze is intermittent and I do not have a deterministic recipe. It has happened several times, each time in this pattern:

1. Run a local gateway as the app-managed service and open the macOS app with the Control UI connected to it ("Local Gateway").
2. Configure a second, remote gateway in the same app. Switch the app from the remote gateway to the local one.
3. Ask a question in an agent, or leave the app idle for a few minutes.
4. Switch to a different group or conversation, then choose **New session**.
5. The UI stops responding to clicks and typing. The window can still be moved. The WebContent process sits at about 100% CPU until the app is quit.

Notes on reliability:

- Two runs that stayed on the local gateway the whole time, including a group switch and **New session**, did not freeze. A two-hour watch with normal use also did not freeze. The failing runs followed a gateway switch or idle time, and the freeze appeared within about a minute of a new WebContent process starting.
- Using the same app on the remote gateway on the same release has not frozen.
- To confirm it, watch the web process while you follow the steps: `ps -axo pid,pcpu,rss,command | grep WebContent | sort -k2 -nr | head`. A process at 100% for more than a few seconds is the loop. Then run `sample <pid> 3` and look for `Element::getAnimations` on the main thread.

### Expected behavior

An idle Control UI should use no CPU. A loop that waits on animations should be bounded, or should stop when the element is hidden or the animation is infinite.

### Actual behavior

he Control UI page enters a busy loop. The page's own JavaScript repeatedly calls `Element.getAnimations()`, and each call forces a full style recalculation. One renderer core sits at 100% or more, and the UI stops responding to clicks and typing. The window can still be moved. Quitting and reopening the app clears it.


### OpenClaw version

2026.11.3

### Operating system

macOS 27.0.1 (both Macbook and Mac mini)

### Install method

mac app

### Model

claude-sonnet_5.5, claude-opus_5.5, ChatGPT_6/Sol_5.5

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw (local gateway). openclaw (remote gateway)

### Additional provider/model setup details

```shell

```

issues.body:
### Summary

On Linux, a single `memory.search.extraPaths` root containing ~100k small `.md` files in ~7.8k directories keeps the Gateway main thread saturated: ~1 core continuously for 15+ hours since start, `eventLoopUtilization` ≈ 0.98–1.0 with `active=0 waiting=0 queued=0`, and 3.2–3.4 GB RSS. The watcher is in native mode (no `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING`, no "fallback polling" warning). A Gateway restart does not help: the load comes back right after startup.

This looks like the Linux/large-tree counterpart of #192629 (Windows, observation boundary, realpath-heavy). There, the cost comes from the boundary being too wide. Here, the boundary is correct but the tree itself is large and receives steady appends.

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.11.3 (847611d), Node 24.22.3, Linux arm64 (Jetson-class box, 6 cores, 7.6 GB RAM)
- `agents.entries.main.memory.search.extraPaths = ["/home/<user>/Docs/.index"]`, global `memory.search.extraPaths = []`
- Tree: 101,963 `.md` files, 7,778 directories, ~565 MB. Layout is `<folder>/<document>/page-NNN.md`, one small file per page so that a chunk equals a page.
- Another process appends ~5–15 files per minute (OCR pipeline). The tree grows steadily and is expected to reach several hundred thousand files.
- The Gateway holds 7,802 inotify watches (≈ one per directory).
- The log shows `Memory file watching is tracking 6726 observed directories…` once per start.

### Evidence

`openclaw gateway call diagnostics.cpuProfile --params '{}'`, two captures of 5 s each (`startBlockedMs` ≈ 2.2 s in both):

| | capture 1 | capture 2 |
|---|---|---|
| inclusive `@openclaw/fs-safe` (top frame) | 79.5% | 57.6% |
| inclusive `lstatSync` (node:fs) | 23.7% | 22.2% |
| inclusive `file-watcher` `exclude` | 8.1% | 5.4% |
| self `[native]` | 62.6% | 61.2% |

Hot path: `processImmediate` / `runNextTicks` → `@openclaw/fs-safe` directory traversal (`readdir`, `lstatSync`, `path.resolve`/`relative`) → `MemoryWatchPolicy.exclude` / `ignored` in `file-watcher-*.mjs` (2026.11.3: `exclude` around line 127, `watch(group.root, { scopes, mode, maxDirectories: 1e6, maxEntries: 1e6, maxPendingPaths: MEMORY_WATCH_MAX_PATHS, exclude, onInvalidate })` around line 320).

Process accounting: 915 min CPU in 935 min wall time. Over 95% of the CPU time is on the main thread. V8 workers are at ~12 min each.

Side effect: `openclaw memory index` from a cron job fails repeatedly with `Cannot admit memory.cli for memory stores … This operation requires exclusive …` (252 times/day).

### Expected

Native watching of a large but correctly scoped tree costs work roughly proportional to the change events, not repeated synchronous traversal of the whole tree on the main thread. Alternatively, there could be a supported way to keep an `extraPaths` root indexed without watching it, for example indexed only by `openclaw memory index`. The docs currently say there is no supported `memory.search.sync.watch` and recommend removing or narrowing the roots. That does not work for a large document corpus that must remain searchable.

### What I have not verified

- Whether the traversal happens with zero appends, i.e. truly idle. The appending process runs most of the day, and I did not stop it on the production box.
- Whether 2026.11.4 changes this. I found nothing obvious in the release notes, but I have not reproduced the problem on it.

### Workaround on our side

We are moving the document index out of `extraPaths` into a separate process, so the Gateway no longer watches the tree.

### Summary
Under the Codex harness, `workboard_complete` (and any OpenClaw tool with a strict schema) cannot run longer than the 90 s dynamic-tool default when a `before_tool_call` hook does real work first. The documented per-call `timeoutMs` extends the watchdog, but the tool then rejects it as an additional property, after the hook has already run. A hook cannot remove the field either, because the `params` a hook returns are merged into the original arguments.

### Version
OpenClaw 2026.11.10 (6ea542f), Codex harness (openai/gpt-6.1-sol), Code Mode on.

### Setup
A plugin registers a gate on card completion:

```js
api.on("before_tool_call", gate, { matcher: ["workboard_complete"], timeoutMs: 1_830_000 });
```

The gate runs the project's test script (2–10 minutes) and blocks the call if the script fails. It passes `ctx.abortSignal` to the script, so a cancelled call stops the script.

### Steps to reproduce
1. A card whose test script sleeps 120 s, then exits 0.
2. The worker calls `workboard_complete({ id, token, summary })`, directly or inside a Code Mode `exec` cell.
   After 90 s: `codex dynamic tool timeout: tool=workboard_complete toolTimeoutMs=90000; per-tool-call watchdog, not session idle`. The abort signal fires, the test script is killed, the card is not completed.
3. The worker calls `workboard_complete({ id, token, summary, timeoutMs: 600000 })`, as `docs/plugins/codex-harness-reference/timeouts.md` describes.
   The watchdog is extended, the hook runs the full 120 s and passes, then: `Invalid arguments for tool "workboard_complete": <root>: must not have additional properties: "timeoutMs".` The card is not completed and the passing test run is lost.
4. The hook returns `{ params: <the arguments without timeoutMs> }`.
   Same error: `mergeParamsWithApprovalOverrides` merges the hook's `params` into the original arguments, so a key cannot be removed.

### Workaround
Calling the tool through the Gateway from a background exec: `openclaw gateway call tools.invoke --timeout 900000 --params '{"name":"workboard_complete", ...}'`. This works, but it puts the claim token on a command line and is much harder for an agent to get right than a plain tool call.

### Expected (any one of these)
- The Codex bridge drops `timeoutMs` / `timeoutSeconds` from the arguments after reading them, when the tool's schema does not declare them.
- The watchdog honours the hook's registered `timeoutMs` (here 1 830 000 ms), or does not count time spent inside `before_tool_call` hooks.
- Tools that can legitimately run long behind a gate hook (`workboard_complete`) accept `timeoutMs` in their schema.

Related: #83966 (closed with "please open a fresh issue on a current release"), #154733 (watchdog blind to approval waits), #201055.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In the Control UI WebChat, photos sent by the agent look blurry in the message and in the enlarged viewer, while the downloaded file is sharp. The `thumbnail` rendition that the chat displays is encoded at one quarter of the requested width for photographic images: requests for 480 / 960 / 1920 px return 120 / 240 / 480 px, and the browser upscales them.

### Steps to reproduce

1. OpenClaw 2026.11.10 on Linux (npm global install).
2. Have the agent send a detailed photo to a Control UI WebChat session (any photographic JPEG or PNG of 1254 px or more on the long side; a `MEDIA:` line in the reply is enough).
3. Compare the image in the message and in the enlarged viewer with the downloaded file.
4. To measure it, request `/api/chat/media/outgoing/<sessionKey>/<attachmentId>/thumbnail?v=4&width=480` (also `960` and `1920`) and read the dimensions of the returned WebP, or call `encodeImageThumbnail(bytes, width)` directly.

### Expected behavior

The rendition's long side equals the requested width (or the source's, when the source is smaller), within the per-width byte budget.

### Actual behavior

The rendition's long side is `width / 4` at every width. Measured by calling `encodeImageThumbnail` from the installed bundle on four photographic sources (JPEG 3804×3804, two JPEGs 1600×1600, PNG 1254×1254); all four gave the same dimensions. Bytes below are for the 3804 px JPEG:

| Requested width | Returned | Bytes | Budget |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 480 | 120×120 | 30,158 | 98,304 |
| 960 | 240×240 | 113,718 | 262,144 |
| 1920 | 480×480 | 426,324 | 524,288 |

The returned files are lossless WebP (`VP8L` chunk). The route answers 200 and nothing is logged.

In the UI this means: the message image (`srcset` 480 at 1x, 960 at 2x) is a 120 px or 240 px bitmap stretched to the bubble, and the enlarged viewer (960 or 1920, by viewport × DPR) shows 240 px or 480 px.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.10 (6ea542f). The same `search` option is on `main` at 535f39d01f69 (read in the source, not run).

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (x86_64), Node v26.13.1

### Install method

npm global

### Model

Not model-specific

### Provider / routing chain

N/A (Gateway HTTP media route and Control UI)

### Additional provider/model setup details

rastermill 0.4.1. On PATH: ImageMagick 6 `convert` and `ffmpeg`; not on PATH: `cwebp`, `vips`, `magick`, `sips`.

### Logs

None. The thumbnail route returns 200 `image/webp`.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Same gateway and same stored attachment, before and after the one-line change described below, requested through the live route (`thumbnail?v=4&width=N`) after a restart:

| Requested width | Before | After | Bytes after | Budget |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 480 | 120×120 | 480×480 | 34,342 | 98,304 |
| 960 | 240×240 | 960×960 | 120,112 | 262,144 |
| 1920 | 480×480 | 1920×1920 | 449,278 | 524,288 |

The "after" files are lossy WebP (`VP8 ` chunk).

### Impact and severity

- Affected: still JPEG/PNG/WebP photos shown in Control UI chat, inline and in the viewer.
- Severity: annoying and misleading. For image work (generated or edited photos) the user judges the result from the chat and concludes that the image itself is low resolution. Here an image was regenerated twice before we found that the preview, not the file, was soft.
- Frequency: always for photographic content on this host.
- Consequence: wasted regeneration time and cost; every image has to be downloaded to be judged.

### Additional information

**Cause.** `encodeImageThumbnail` ([`src/gateway/managed-image-thumbnail-cache.ts` L32-L41 @ v2026.11.10](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.11.10/src/gateway/managed-image-thumbnail-cache.ts#L32-L41)) encodes WebP under `CHAT_IMAGE_RENDITION_MAX_BYTES` and searches only over the side:

```ts
search: { maxSide: [width, width / 2, width / 4] },
```

With no quality candidates the WebP comes out lossless, about 1.9 bytes per pixel for a photo. The budgets grow 96 → 256 → 512 KB while the pixel count grows 4× per step, so a photo fits neither at `width` nor at `width / 2` and lands on `width / 4` at every width. For width 480: 480² ≈ 426 KB and 240² ≈ 114 KB both exceed 96 KB; 120² ≈ 30 KB fits.

**Local workaround.** Adding quality candidates to the same call in the installed bundle:

```ts
search: { maxSide: [width, width / 2, width / 4], quality: [90, 84, 78, 72, 66, 60, 52] },
```

gives the full requested side at quality 90 inside the same budgets (table above). The source comment in v2026.11.10 says that specifying quality would require an external codec. On this host the quality search worked; I did not determine which rastermill backend produced the lossy output, so this exact change may not be portable.

**Suggestions.**

- Add quality candidates when a lossy-capable backend is available; otherwise fall back to JPEG for opaque images (the HEIF path on `main` already returns JPEG) instead of dropping to `width / 4`.
- Add a test with a photographic fixture that asserts the output long side equals the requested width. The current test file covers queueing and the unsupported-format error, not output dimensions.
- Bump the `v=4` cache-buster of the rendition URL with the fix. The responses carry `cache-control: private, max-age=31536000, immutable`, so browsers keep the quarter-size renditions they already fetched.

Related: #173161 (lightweight chat image renditions), #203585 (HEIC previews, same function).

## Summary
Separate shared Android data and policy from feature-specific owners, consolidating demonstrated duplicate implementations while preserving app behavior.

## Problem to solve
Generic JSON accessors live beside node invocation helpers even though chat, Gateway parsing, settings, voice and Wear consume them. Chat model identity policy also lives in a Compose picker but is used by controllers. Talk route parsing imports a model predicate from setup readiness while readiness imports that parser back. These dependencies make otherwise independent app logic harder to change and test.

## Proposed solution
Use the existing shared data owners, migrate every affected caller, and remove replaced implementations. Deliver narrow PRs with source/history evidence, focused Android validation and independent review.

Initial candidates:
- Move unchanged generic JSON accessors to the existing shared JSON owner.
- Move cron list parsing and summary contracts from runtime orchestration into the existing cron data owner.
- Consolidate model identity policy outside the picker.
- Remove the Talk config/readiness dependency cycle.

## Rejected consolidation candidates

Wear text projections accept different malformed-input shapes, so merging them directly would change behavior. Installed-skill readiness predicates are already shared; an additional classifier would add complexity for a negligible reduction.

## Impact and compatibility
Internal maintenance work; no intended user-visible behavior, protocol, permission, credential, persistence or dependency changes. Releases and deployments are outside scope.

## Alternatives considered
Keep feature-local helpers when their semantics differ. Avoid broad extraction-only rewrites, duplicate compatibility aliases and new abstractions without a concrete responsibility.

## Implementation intent
Maintainer-requested cleanup campaign. Each PR will link this issue and record its own validation and compatibility evidence.

## Delivery status

Remote-verified merges: **20/120** — Contracts/chat 11/40, Settings/domain 6/40, Voice/Wear 3/40. The original target remains unchanged. All twenty PRs have verified remote merges and native completion.

The latest two changes have verified remote merges.
