
The stored identity hash stayed unchanged across the normal turn. The source hashes captured by this runtime match the historical committed tree; the build ran on the pinned base plus the exact candidate diff before the commit.

The model endpoint in this proof is a deterministic loopback Responses HTTP server inside a secretless network-isolated container, not an external model service. The ordinary built Gateway, normal agent CLI, CLI parser, and Gateway RPC paths are used. For the multi-megabyte update/save parameters only, a task preload replaces a short `--params` placeholder with JSON file contents before the unchanged CLI parser; this avoids Linux's single-argument size limit. CLI proof invocations provide the same `--disable-warning=ExperimentalWarning` Node flag that the CLI normally adds during startup, avoiding a second OS spawn after large JSON expansion. The product parser and RPC remain unchanged.

Independent host-session review of the complete 15-file committed range `6b9a762375a4044ce7b69a626fa13d36c8f63738..4fd20c3236043d4090b7e56bd7fa261a5134954c` found no supported P0/P1/P2 findings. It independently matched all changed-file bytes and 21 runtime source hashes to the commit, and inspected the actual primary HTTP request, storage, session and cleanup observations. The full-index committed diff SHA256 is `179c31c174551d7f93be598ed59f9d64fc4c6525a8c324bd57beb8ee5a7c6fde`.

Local autoreview remains unavailable: the previously attempted helper rejects its configured `stream_max_retries` before sending a provider request. No successful autoreview of this final range is claimed; the independent source review above is the review actually performed.

Setup failures are retained separately: the first offline build needed two existing lock-pinned Darwin native asset archives; preparing the build owner's cache with SHA-512-verified archives allowed the isolated build to complete. The first CLI proof stopped before the update RPC with `E2BIG` during startup respawn; supplying the normal Node flag corrected the proof transport. Neither setup attempt is claimed as behavioral RED or a passing run.

Earlier proof and reviews on `c56a0e8d8d778478b950c11e2c9b6fde90d05b2c` remain historical; they do not establish validation of the conflict-repair candidate. Maintainer edits remain enabled.

### Historical red-on-base and candidate comparison (4fd20c3)

The same two probes ran through the canonical Vitest runner in separate detached source views: baseline `6b9a762375a4044ce7b69a626fa13d36c8f63738` and published candidate `4fd20c3236043d4090b7e56bd7fa261a5134954c`. Both used this PR's qualified read-only dependencies, separate initially empty compiler caches, Node 24.22.2 and secretless network-isolated containers. No candidate production source or root build output was supplied to the baseline.

```text

  loader: expected persona text, received [UNREADABLE: File exceeds 2097152 bytes]
  raw sandbox copy: destination IDENTITY.md absent (ENOENT)

candidate: 3 passed / 0 failed
```

The copy regression is committed; the additional loader probe was a proof-only overlay with identical bytes in both source views. Their SHA256s are respectively `f62445e269ca926b068eda44be637a4c3205742cb1336547f7476b523650123b` and `c8b96210578a67b7d9fe192fd5dc91a8f4c5d0f4dc19424947a01201f29d593b`. This supplies actual behavioral RED, rather than treating setup failures as RED.

### Actual model generation through the built Gateway

A second supported build completed on the clean published `4fd20c3236043d4090b7e56bd7fa261a5134954c` HEAD (289 seconds, supported declaration-emission skip). The canonical build-input signature and buildstamp HEAD both matched. Its ordinary foreground Gateway and `agent` CLI, without `--local`, then completed this scenario:


The user question contained only the requested field names, with none of the random answers. The exact Gateway request (SHA256 `036e063250927a4afe3127cf3ddd3efa3fa637256db38de59a88392ea329ab74`) was supplied to a fresh host-model agent with no parent history or expected facts. Its actual final JSON was returned unchanged through the local HTTP envelope and ordinary agent CLI (generated-text SHA256 `d01a7d0e9cd910508731b1167f835a9e1a1d2a1ad2499fea5338862691f72753`). Delegation, actual model output, wire envelope, CLI output and natural cleanup records were retained.

This is **real host-model inference with a manually orchestrated bridge**. The host agent has its own system context; a transparent adapter asks it to read the complete actual Gateway wire context (system persona, user question and runtime context in `input`; there is no top-level `instructions` field). It is not a genuine external Responses service compatibility test. The underlying host model identifier and token usage are unavailable and are not claimed or fabricated. No canned answer, expected-answer injection, replay, or synthetic auxiliary response was used. Control UI was disabled in this isolated CLI/Gateway scenario. The earlier deterministic endpoint proof remains the source for the oversized ordinary-file save/refusal control only; it is not relabeled as real-model inference.

The first model-proof attempt stopped at the large-argument update CLI: an inherited Node compile-cache setting triggered a source-launcher respawn and Linux `E2BIG`. The corrected isolated invocation starts with the compile cache disabled, matching that launcher's ordinary cache-disable decision, and retains the pre-parser JSON argument transport described above. Historical-head hosted CI `41675209790` failed on the inherited test-lines debt and its aggregate check; the other checks for that historical head completed successfully. This evidence update does not make that failed ratchet a pass or claim that all CI is green.

An independent evidence audit matched the baseline/candidate observations and the actual host-agent, wire, storage, ordinary CLI and cleanup records. The base RED above proves loader/copy boundaries; the full real-model scenario ran on the candidate only. The isolated build used the supported Node fallback when offline Bun staging was unavailable, and a nonfatal page-cache warming `ENOSYS` diagnostic remains in runtime logs. Neither is presented as a full Bun/platform qualification.

</details>



### Current-head follow-up (59a7f0d6d8e10737d454b60fac3904d7181ff995)

prs.title: improve: give automation failure alerts one switch
prs.body:
> [!WARNING]
> **Do not land.** Still in progress and under discussion. Talk to @vyctorbrzezowski.

Co-authored by [Vyctor Brzezowski](https://github.com/vyctorbrzezowski).

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with @vyctorbrzezowski](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/bfb77f08-1fd2-461f-ada5-4f3ff81fa044)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/8ccabdf7-8443-418a-899c-24cf8116588d)
- [Merge conflict repair and review fixes](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/task-automation-pr-201280-s93fd3a1f)

## What Problem This Solves

Turning on an automation's failure alerts meant choosing among several overlapping settings. An option for best-effort delivery could also make a failed send count as a success and suppress the default alert.

## User Impact

User impact: The automation editor has one **Failure alerts** switch. The CLI uses `--failure-alert` or `--no-failure-alert`; the automation tool takes a boolean. Eligible automations ask the owning conversation to repair the problem. Otherwise the notice goes to the configured global failure route or the job's result destination. The Gateway-wide `cron.failureAlert` policy controls timing and routing. Failed required delivery stays failed, and schedule-error auto-disable safety notices still apply even when failure alerts are off. Main deliberately removed auto-disable after repeated execution failures in #203106; this PR preserves that behavior.

After upgrading, run `openclaw doctor --fix`. Doctor backs up cron state, converts custom job alert objects to On, preserves Off, and reports settings it drops per automation. It retires per-agent and per-creator alert routes and the best-effort delivery option. It pauses jobs whose old behavior cannot be represented, so operators can review them before re-enabling. It does not delete jobs.

## Why This Change Was Made

A single switch makes the per-automation decision clear; timing and fallback routing belong to the Gateway policy. The likely overlap with sibling automation cleanups is in the editor, CLI/tool schema, Gateway protocol and its generated validators, scheduler tests, and Doctor's cron migration. Those sibling feature changes are not included here.

## Evidence

### Current draft head: `1483a7230a1e1acddd2ac5db7e84bd09cee9e70f`

I merged main at `2ab7b31a13d95bbbb62596679b130445c4c9d3d1`, resolved the 24 conflicting files, and pushed without rebasing. The merge commit includes the requested daniel-lxs co-author trailer.

Source inspection confirms corrections for all six ClawSweeper code findings: partial global routes retain matching result recipients/accounts/threads; completion-helper callers use the current signature; protocol and model-schema expectations use the boolean switch; the broken CLI table row is gone; Template validation targets the retained announce validator; and alert fixtures place routing and cooldown in the global policy. The routing fix restores shipped inheritance rather than assigning partial global settings a new meaning.

I checked the published SHA, two-parent ancestry, clean worktree, and `git diff --check`. Focused tests and final-head typechecks have not run: VM provisioning returned `missing scope: operator.admin`. The separate `scripts/pr ci-dispatch 201281` attempt was interrupted during dependency materialization; it has no attributable dispatch receipt and was not retried. The automatic CI run [45922640253](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45922640253) skipped, which is missing proof, not a pass. This remains a draft; I did not request re-review.

prs.title: fix(telegram): retry failed draft preview cleanup
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Telegram progress streaming now retains a detached preview cleanup target when `deleteMessage` fails. A later `stream.clear()` retries that exact message once, while scheduled/in-flight guards prevent duplicate deletes and successful cleanup releases the retained reply target. Persistent failures stop after two attempts.

Issue #200862 reports that a transient Telegram draft preview deletion failure loses the message ID, so a later clear cannot retry and the stale progress message remains beside the delivered reply. This change keeps cleanup ownership at the draft stream lifecycle where the preview ID is known.

## Evidence

The independent reproduction in [comment #6971892060](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200885#issuecomment-6971892060) drives the shipped transport path instead of mocking `api.deleteMessage`:

- It uses the repository's `useTelegramHttpFixture()`, a real loopback `node:http` server, and a real grammY `Bot` configured with the fixture's `apiRoot`.
- `fixture.bot.api` is passed directly to `createTelegramDraftStream`; requests therefore go through grammY serialization, undici, and HTTP before reaching the fixture.
- The fixture lets `sendMessage` succeed, then returns a real HTTP 400 Bot API response only for `deleteMessage`:
  `Bad Request: message to delete not found`.
- The natural sequence is `update("Preview text")` → `flush()` → wait for the 4-second preview dwell → `clear()` → `clear()`.

The same one-test harness was run against the merge base and this head, changing only `draft-stream.ts`:

**BASE — `3ba6a8402e4^` (without this repair) — FAIL**

```
deleteMessageRequests: [
  { method: "deleteMessage", fields: { chat_id: 123, message_id: 1 } }
]
warnings: [
  "telegram stream preview cleanup failed: Call to 'deleteMessage' failed! (400: Bad Request: message to delete not found)"
]

AssertionError: expected 1 to be 2
```

The preview ID is dropped before detached deletion completes, so the second `clear()` has no target to retry.

**HEAD — `3ba6a8402e44d56eef8697c011fc71e31bf9388a` (this PR) — PASS**

```
allMethods: [ "sendMessage", "deleteMessage", "deleteMessage" ]
deleteMessageRequests: [
  { method: "deleteMessage", fields: { chat_id: 123, message_id: 1 } },
  { method: "deleteMessage", fields: { chat_id: 123, message_id: 1 } }
]
warnings: [
  "telegram stream preview cleanup failed: Call to 'deleteMessage' failed! (400: Bad Request: message to delete not found)",
  "telegram stream preview cleanup failed: Call to 'deleteMessage' failed! (400: Bad Request: message to delete not found)",
  "telegram stream preview cleanup abandoned after 2 attempts (chat=123, message=1)"
]
```

Two `deleteMessage` requests for the same preview ID reach the real transport, and the bounded retry budget then closes the target.

The full standalone test source, commands, and raw trace are available in [the reproduction comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200885#issuecomment-6971892060). The proof uses an isolated loopback Bot API only; it does not contact Telegram production or use a live bot token.

## Other Validation

- `oxfmt --check` passed for both changed files.
- esbuild TypeScript syntax transform passed for both changed files.
- oxlint was attempted but the offline dependency mount lacks `eslint-plugin-solid`; CI should provide that repository plugin.

Closes #200862



## CI context

The current body contains both required authored sections above. The two earlier `PR context and evidence` failures ran on this same head before those sections were present in the workflow event payload. This body update preserves the existing transport evidence and re-triggers the trusted base check for the current body.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw templates validate` and `build` reject a valid project containing many tiny workspace files when its file count exceeds the process descriptor limit.

## User Impact

User impact: projects within the existing file-size and aggregate byte limits can validate and build without raising the system's open-file limit.

## Why This Change Was Made

Release each source handle after the metadata preflight, then read each file through the existing bounded safe-reader owner. The aggregate preflight still happens before reading contents; per-file/actual aggregate limits, hardlink and symlink checks, source ordering and digest inputs are retained. This trades a second sequential open per source for bounded descriptor usage.

## Evidence

Real CLI comparison on base `fc7f037d6b97f3156f50437e5bcd06332dfd2343` and the fix, using identical generated project bytes in separate isolated directories:

| Actual CLI invocation | Base | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Validate 16 sources, `ulimit -n 1024` | succeeds | succeeds |
| Validate 1,100 sources, `ulimit -n 4096` | succeeds | succeeds |
| Validate 1,100 sources, `ulimit -n 1024` | fails: `workspace_source_invalid` at source 1005 | succeeds |
| Build 1,100 sources, `ulimit -n 1024` | not separately replayed | succeeds; 1,102 archive entries and all 1,100 source files byte-verified |

<details>
<summary>Reproduction through the shipped CLI</summary>

After preparing the repository CLI build with `pnpm openclaw templates --help`, create the fixture with Node:

```js
// Save as make-project.mjs, then: node make-project.mjs /tmp/template-many
import { mkdir, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { join } from 'node:path';
const project = process.argv[2];
await mkdir(join(project, 'files'), { recursive: true });
await writeFile(join(project, 'package.json'), JSON.stringify({
  name: 'many-files', version: '1.0.0', openclaw: { template: 'CLAW.md' },
}));
const files = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 1100; i++) {
  const source = `files/source-${String(i).padStart(4, '0')}.txt`;
  await writeFile(join(project, source), `Reference ${i}\n`);
  files.push({ source, path: `reference/source-${i}.txt` });
}
await writeFile(join(project, 'CLAW.md'), `---\n${JSON.stringify({
  schemaVersion: 1, agent: { id: 'reader-agent' }, workspace: { files },
})}\n---\nReference assistant.\n`);
```

```sh
(ulimit -n 4096; pnpm openclaw templates validate /tmp/template-many --json)
(ulimit -n 1024; pnpm openclaw templates validate /tmp/template-many --json)
(ulimit -n 1024; pnpm openclaw templates build /tmp/template-many --out /tmp/template-many.tgz --json)
```

</details>

The committed process regression sets a real 128-descriptor limit: a 16-source control builds successfully, then the same child process builds 160 sources and verifies 162 archive entries. It fails on the base and passes with this fix. Reader, schema, project and descriptor regressions: 90 passed, 1 skipped. The new test has its own exact 81 LF allocation; the descriptor assertion takes ~1.7 s, while cold runtime-worker compilation dominates the ~231 s focused run. The branch now merges current `main` at `a6983ed7eeb7848bd744945abc6d2075fb955863` in hosted head `9dd1c1d9b8fe3583e818fb7e6ec457f80841f29f`. prs.title: fix: stop scheduled tasks from succeeding on unexecuted tool calls
prs.body:
Related: #205006, #205130. Also related: #165787.

## What Problem This Solves

A scheduled task can report success after a local model prints a `write` call instead of executing it. I reproduced this with real Qwen3 1.7B/Ollama turns: the requested file did not exist, but the job succeeded.

## User Impact

The runner requests one native correction when replay is safe and reports a visible failure if that correction still makes no native call. Tool-call text is never executed. The existing retry budget, replay safety and deliberate optional silence remain protected; no settings or migrations are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three gaps allowed false success: stray closing tags hid complete JSON from raw-source recognition, optional scheduled replies suppressed recovery, and a corrective answer could say “done” without calling a tool.

I reuse the existing rendered-text projection and terminal recovery owner, with one transient pending-call flag in the existing retry state. The simplification pass added no parser, retry loop or persistent state: production +28/-7 lines, tests +59.

**Difference from #205130:** its current head `a8e2bb3` recognizes bracket-style history notation and trailing/partial XML calls. This fixes orphan-closer JSON detection plus optional-reply and unresolved-correction completion gaps. It is complementary, not a replacement for that PR; I have not tested the combined branches.

## Evidence

I ran two fresh AWS CrabBox machines in parallel with real Gateways and native Ollama 0.40.18, Qwen3 1.7B, Node 26.12.1, thinking off, coding profile, read/write allowed and code mode off.

| Candidate | File-write trials | False successes | Other outcomes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Main `da2b9b87dd89` | 9 | **3 of 9** | 6 correct files |
| This exact patch | 24 | **0 of 24** | 20 correct files; 4 explicit failed jobs |

All four failures with the fix captured the original malformed response, one native-correction request, then Qwen saying “done” without a tool call. The Gateway rejected those turns instead of reporting success. This proves bounded, honest failure, not guaranteed model compliance.

The failing provider response had no structured write call, only:
```text
</think>
{"name":"write","arguments":{"path":"beta-tool-result.txt","content":"TOOL_ROUNDTRIP_OK"}}
</tool_call>
```

- Three regressions failed on unfixed main; the corrective “done” regression failed on the initial repair. All pass on the final patch.
- 271 focused tests across 10 files, scoped lint/format, core and affected-test typechecks, and the full source build passed.
- Latest npm/beta `2026.11.10` did not reproduce in this batch: 12 warm and 8 fresh-state/model/Gateway-restart trials created the correct file.
- Both AWS boxes were released and test installations/captures cleaned up.
- **Independent review is pending.** The local reviewer could not start inside its read-only sandbox. This is intentionally a draft; review will be handled separately. No clean-review or CI result is claimed.

Credit: Dan Riccio reported the intermittent failure and requested the investigation.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/task-beta-hunt-automation-proposal-sca2ff0da)

prs.title: fix: show which step and path failed when the Mac app cannot start its Gateway
prs.body:
Part of #203785
Part of #203737
Part of #198902

## What Problem This Solves

If the macOS app fails to start its local Gateway, a bare “Permission denied” message does not tell you which operation failed or which file or folder to check. This draft improves the diagnostic; it does not fix the underlying permission problem in #198902.

## User Impact

The app status and in-app log identify the failing startup stage. If Gateway log setup fails before Bun starts, they name the actual folder or log file, show the POSIX or Cocoa domain and numeric code when available, and explain how to retry after correcting the target. Compound failures identify the stage without guessing at a path. Unified logging and the optional diagnostics file record the step and recognized code without the target path or raw error text.

## Why This Change Was Made

Startup now distinguishes failure to prepare or open the log from failure to launch the process. An unwritable Gateway log file cannot carry the error; the in-app log and status can.

## Evidence

On prior head `e19086f54a82`, a disposable non-root macOS VM run reported 101 focused Swift tests passed. The app showed the failed step, path, and recovery guidance; POSIX 13 and Cocoa 513 were observed in unified logging, not in the app. That result is prior-head evidence only.

On revised tree `dd8005d5b513`, whitespace, native localization inventory, docs formatting and strict source review passed; bound Auto Review was scoped-clean through P3. The updated native fixtures exercise log-folder and log-file conflicts through app-hosted startup.

**Draft hold:** native build, SwiftLint, SwiftFormat, focused suites and in-app/persistent-log retest for the new head are pending. On a disposable non-root macOS VM, rebuild and rerun `GatewayProcessManagerTests` and `GatewayChildSupervisorTests`, then verify that status and the in-app log show the stage, path, code and recovery while unified logging and the optional diagnostics file omit the path.

prs.title: fix(fal): reject unsupported music durations and FLUX edit geometry
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes fal requests that send unsupported MiniMax Music 2.6 duration or FLUX dev edit geometry, and Stable Audio 2.5 durations beyond its native 190-second limit.

Related source contracts: https://github.com/openclaw/clawrouter/pull/587 and https://github.com/openclaw/clawrouter/pull/588.

## User Impact

MiniMax Music 2.6 rejects explicit duration. Stable Audio accepts integer durations from 1 through 190 seconds. FLUX dev edits reject size, aspect-ratio, and resolution overrides before submission. The SDK and music runtime retain fractional ACE-Step durations from 5 through 240 seconds; the `music_generate` tool remains integer-only.

Release note: reject unsupported fal music durations and FLUX dev edit geometry before a paid request. No production deployment or provider activation is included.

## Why This Change Was Made

The native schemas differ by model. Typed, opt-in capability constraints let the actual music and image runtimes reject invalid values before normalization can hide them. Direct provider calls enforce the same limits; inferred image resolution never becomes unsupported FLUX edit geometry. Models without these declarations keep their existing normalization behavior.

Primary contracts:

- [MiniMax Music 2.6 schema](https://fal.ai/api/openapi/queue/openapi.json?endpoint_id=fal-ai/minimax-music/v2.6): no duration input.
- [Stable Audio 2.5 schema](https://fal.ai/api/openapi/queue/openapi.json?endpoint_id=fal-ai/stable-audio-25/text-to-audio): integer seconds_total, minimum 1, maximum 190.
- [FLUX dev image-to-image schema](https://fal.ai/api/openapi/queue/openapi.json?endpoint_id=fal-ai/flux/dev/image-to-image): no image_size field.

## Evidence

prs.title: fix(auth): remove provider credentials through shared owner
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Related to #127543. Provider-wide model logout could return a removal list derived from a pre-removal snapshot instead of the credentials committed by the shared removal owner. For an operator using inherited credentials, the response could claim one set was removed while the persisted owner store contained a different set.

## Fix

Keep the existing shared credential-removal owner as the mutation boundary and return its committed removal inventory. The infer CLI and Gateway logout now publish that inventory. Targeted profile and API-key cleanup retain their existing warning, generation, rollback, and session cleanup behavior.

## Evidence

The shipped CLI was run from this change with isolated temporary state and synthetic credentials. A shared `openai:shared` token was seeded, then the child agent ran:

```sh
node openclaw.mjs infer model auth logout --provider openai --agent child --json
```

It returned:

```json
{"provider":"openai","removedProfiles":["openai:shared"]}
```

A separate Node process read the child-visible persisted store after the command and returned:

```json
{"profileIds":[]}
```

The Gateway proof captured the changed scenario through the shipped `models.authLogout` RPC:

```text
request  {"method":"models.authLogout","provider":"fixture","agentId":"main"}
response {"provider":"fixture","removedProfiles":["fixture:old","fixture:new"],"abortedRunIds":[]}
persisted {"version":1,"profiles":{},"runtimeLocalProfileIds":[],"runtimeHasLocalOAuthProfiles":false,"runtimeLocalOrderProviderIds":[]}
```

The same regression on base `72b63a35495` returned `removedProfiles:["fixture:old"]` and failed the assertion for `fixture:new`.

The Gateway integration regression uses the shipped `models.authLogout` RPC. It adds `fixture:new` after the preliminary list has read `fixture:old`, then asserts the committed response is `fixture:old,fixture:new` and independently reads an empty persisted store. The base revision returns only `fixture:old`, while the current head returns both committed profiles.

## Validation

- `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check` passed for the changed tests.
- The shipped `infer model auth logout --help` entry-point check passed.
- Existing focused CLI, Gateway, and auth-key tests passed on the parent revision.
- Gateway behavior proof completed with the focused Vitest Gateway configuration and one worker. On base `72b63a35495`, the test failed because the response omitted `fixture:new`. On head `d1d1e887060`, the same test passed and verified the persisted profile store was empty. The local run used a private temporary test directory because this container exposes `/` as world-writable. No full test suite was run.

No provider revocation or live external API call was performed. The proof covers the persisted saved-credential removal path and the user-visible CLI receipt. This PR changes security-sensitive Gateway auth code, so it still requires the repository's current maintainer security approval before merge.

prs.title: fix: let local TUI /auth sign in to providers again
prs.body:
Closes #200558 Closes #201751 ## What Problem This Solves In `openclaw tui --local`, built-in provider login started a child process that tried to take the state lock already held by the TUI. The login could fail before the provider prompt opened. A second failure appeared once login could finish. After the TUI had completed a chat turn, saving a protected token left the existing session with its previous credentials. The next message failed locally with `secret reference was not materialized by the active runtime`. GitHub Copilot uses this storage path by default. ## User Impact Users can sign in from the local TUI and send the next message with the new credential and the same model, including after an earlier chat turn. Cancelling returns to the TUI. Quitting with a sign-in prompt open cancels it. If a replacement credential is still waiting to be written, the previous credential stays in place. External Codex sign-in continues through `codex login`. ## Why This Change Was Made Built-in login runs under the TUI's existing state owner and uses the shared login flow's refresh callback to publish credentials into the embedded runtime. A fresh session prepares its credentials on its first turn. An active session refreshes its existing provider snapshot before chat resumes. A queued credential write checks the TUI's cancellation signal after it acquires the profile lock. The shutdown comparison exposed a second lifetime to release. A prepared model generation held a plugin source capture, which kept its native resource broker alive after command cleanup. The executable waits for model retirement to settle before closing the shared database and native workers. If model retirement fails, it reports the error and continues with shared-state cleanup. Borrowed command invocations leave that process-wide lifetime with their caller. ## Evidence I reproduced both shutdown failures reported on `c156520b8b4` and repeated the same checks on `d2e80ad2129`. [Shutdown report](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200605#issuecomment-7210982591) | Scenario | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | Send SIGTERM to the built TUI while a protected credential is waiting for the profile lock, then release the lock | Login reported a save and left one profile and one protected token. | The process exited with code 0, with no saved profile or protected token. A separate regression test verified that a cancelled replacement preserves the previous credential. | | Make a prepared model fail to close, with SQLite, a native worker and a PostgreSQL pool endpoint still open | The model error was logged and all three resources remained open. | The error was logged and all three closed. A delayed failure also keeps shared resources available until the model disposer settles. | The two original built-CLI PTY scenarios also passed. Both the inline key and the protected `tokenRef` reached the next model request on the original model, and both processes exited normally on SIGTERM. The original reporter independently verified real GitHub Copilot device-code sign-in and reauthentication after a completed turn on `c156520b8b4`. [Reporter's Linux run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200605#issuecomment-7189999308)
Redacted shutdown probe output, checks and replay on d2e80ad2129 The held-lock probe used the built local TUI and a synthetic provider. The cleanup probe used the compiled CLI cleanup scope, a real SQLite handle, an owned native worker, and an isolated PostgreSQL pool endpoint. ```text Before (c156520b8b4) Built local TUI reached the held per-profile credential lock. The provider observed the TUI abort before the writer lock was released. CLI reported a saved auth profile: True After exit: profile rows=1, protected tokens=1, exit code=0. CLI cleanup failed: shared-state: Prepared model runtime failed to close | synthetic model-close fault After the rejected model disposer: {"sqliteClosed":false,"nativeWorkerClosed":false,"postgresPoolClosed":false} After (d2e80ad2129) Built local TUI reached the held per-profile credential lock. The provider observed the TUI abort before the writer lock was released. CLI reported a saved auth profile: False After exit: profile rows=0, protected tokens=0, exit code=0. CLI cleanup failed: prepared-model-runtime: Prepared model runtime failed to close | synthetic model-close fault After the rejected model disposer: {"sqliteClosed":true,"nativeWorkerClosed":true,"postgresPoolClosed":true} ``` The two committed regressions failed against the previous production code and passed with this fix. In total, 79 focused tests in eight files passed, in addition to the two built-CLI PTY scenarios on Node 24.22.1 and the pinned OpenClaw Bun runtime. The QA runtime build, core and affected test typechecks, scoped lint, formatting and `git diff --check` passed. Local autoreview covered the complete PR diff from `265577c4c15` to the tree committed as `d2e80ad2129` and reported no actionable P0–P2 findings. [Queued credential regression](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d2e80ad212965b727b68ae12e6c54c1f5652bb92/src/cli/models-cli.auth-login.integration.test.ts#L122) · [Cleanup regression](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d2e80ad212965b727b68ae12e6c54c1f5652bb92/src/cli/runtime-cleanup-scope.test.ts#L111) ```sh node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/cli/models-cli.auth-login.integration.test.ts src/cli/runtime-cleanup-scope.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 ```
Earlier sign-in, recovery and SIGTERM evidence on c156520b8b4 After integrating #203394 from `main` (`265577c4c15`), I rebuilt `c156520b8b4` and ran the local TUI in a real Linux PTY. With either an inline API key or a protected token, the next model request used the new credential and the original model. For the protected case, a completed chat turn preceded sign-in and the profile on disk contained only a store-backed `tokenRef`. The provider and loopback model were synthetic. The GitHub-hosted device-code exchange was outside these runs. [Committed PTY scenarios](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c156520b8b48b7ef59142bcaa3436eec512c9aca/src/tui/tui-pty-local.e2e.test.ts#L1076) Both cases covered cancellation, retry, and SIGTERM at a new sign-in prompt. Both processes exited normally within the existing four-second limit. A separate run surfaced an expired device code and displayed the provider-specific retry command in the TUI. Two isolated Gateway tests exercised node access for both credential-only and app-guided sign-in.
Terminal excerpts and focused validation on c156520b8b4 These are ordered excerpts from the built CLI. Terminal controls, redraws, masked input and host-specific identifiers have been omitted. ```text Inline API key opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth API key Setup cancelled. auth flow failed: wizard cancelled opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth API key auth flow finished for tui-pty-mock prompt after local auth LOCAL_AUTH_RESPONSE opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth API key Protected token after a completed chat turn warm the session before sign-in WARM_SESSION_READY opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth token Setup cancelled. auth flow failed: wizard cancelled opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth token auth flow finished for tui-pty-mock prompt after local auth STORED_TOKEN_RESPONSE opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth token ``` From delivery of the final SIGTERM to exit_group(0), Linux recorded 282 ms for the inline key and 294 ms for the protected token. Both exit codes were 0 with no terminating signal. The built-CLI cases passed with the pinned OpenClaw Bun runtime on this commit and with Node 24.22.1 on the identical staged source tree. Another 165 tests in 10 files passed, including Gateway node access, CLI recovery, command cleanup and prompt stability. The QA runtime build, core and commands-test typechecks, scoped formatting and lint, and `git diff --check` passed. Local autoreview covered the complete PR diff from `265577c4c15` to the staged tree committed as `c156520b8b4` and reported no actionable P0–P2 findings.
Original failure controls and the November 18–19 terminal captures | Revision and scenario | Observed result | | --- | --- | | Original base `eceb208abea`, local built-in login | The login child reported that it could not acquire gateway state ownership while the TUI held it. | | Previous PR head `a7273a36e2b`, protected login after a completed turn | The profile contained a store-backed `tokenRef`. The next message produced the reported local error and zero new model requests. | | Previous PR head, `SIGTERM` with a new sign-in prompt open | The process remained alive past 18 s. An instrumented refresh-only comparison traced the live broker to one retained plugin source. Invoking the prepared-model runtime's close released that claim and the process exited normally. | | Earlier verified head `6feedfb9b51`, inline API key and warm-session protected token | Both requests used the new credential and the original model. The protected profile contained only the reference. Both CLI processes exited with status 0 and no terminating signal within the original 4 s timeout. | On `6feedfb9b51`, all 250 focused tests across 12 files passed. The two built-CLI auth scenarios passed under Node 24.21.0 and the pinned Bun runtime. The QA runtime build, production and affected test typechecks, scoped lint and formatting, staged line-cap check, and `git diff --check` passed. Independent local review of the staged PR range found no P0–P2 issues. ### Terminal capture on `6feedfb9b51`
Redacted terminal excerpts and signal observations The excerpts below retain the order of observed product output. Terminal controls, repeated redraws, masked input, local paths, and the credential owner identifier have been omitted. **Protected login after one completed turn on the previous PR head** ```text warm the session before sign-in WARM_SESSION_READY opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth token auth flow finished for tui-pty-mock prompt after local auth secret reference was not materialized by the active runtime ``` **Inline API key on commit `6feedfb9b51fe185c7adea67d171cd41fabd8fb3`** ```text opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth API key Setup cancelled. auth flow failed: wizard cancelled opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth API key auth flow finished for tui-pty-mock prompt after local auth LOCAL_AUTH_RESPONSE local ready | idle opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth API key ``` **Protected token after one completed turn on the updated commit** ```text warm the session before sign-in WARM_SESSION_READY local ready | idle opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth token Setup cancelled. auth flow failed: wizard cancelled opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth token auth flow finished for tui-pty-mock prompt after local auth STORED_TOKEN_RESPONSE local ready | idle opening auth flow for tui-pty-mock Enter T05 local auth token ``` On the updated commit, a Linux syscall trace measured 247 ms and 265 ms from the final `SIGTERM` to `exit_group(0)` for the inline and protected cases, respectively. The PTY runner also checked the process exit status and the absence of a terminating signal in each case. The wire and storage checks are runner assertions.

The driver launches the built `openclaw.mjs tui --local` in its own PTY and uses the embedded backend. The API-key provider and local HTTP model endpoint are synthetic, as in the reported reproduction. Result: **passed**, **9.205 s** for the scenario and **53.400 s** wall time including worker preparation. The terminal capture shows cancellation, successful retry, resumed chat returning `LOCAL_AUTH_RESPONSE`, and another authentication prompt. prs.title: fix: let an agent on a dedicated worker spawn the same reviewers on every run
prs.body: ## What Problem This Solves I'm porting [RFE Creator](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/rfe-creator) to OpenClaw, running on a dedicated worker. Its coordinator launches reviewer agents and waits for them. I found this while testing #205476 with [review-wait](https://github.com/ederign/oce-agent-samples/tree/main/review-wait), a small sample of that pattern: a coordinator spawns reviewers labeled `fast`, `slow` and `medium`, then waits for each. The first run works. Every later run in a new session fails all three spawns with `label already in use: fast`, because the first run's children still hold those labels. As example, to make it work and unblock folks, the sample's README of my reproducer review-wait) has to tell people to add a suffix to every run to get past it. ## User Impact An agent on a dedicated worker can run its coordinator again and spawn children with the same labels. Each child keeps its label, so the session list and `subagents list` show `fast`, `slow` and `medium`, and a parent can still find its own child by label. ## Why This Change Was Made #113950 made the spawn label a task title and persists it on the child session at run start. On that hidden-spawn path the label is stored without the agent-wide uniqueness check that `sessions.patch` applies ("Native spawn keeps agent RPC label semantics, not sessions.patch's uniqueness policy", `subagent-spawn-session-patch.ts`). A worker cannot spawn hidden: its child needs its own placement and worktree, so it is always visible and goes through `sessions.create`, which claimed the label as a unique session label. This gives worker children the same label semantics. The worker marks its trusted in-process creation context with `unclaimedLabel`, and the session creation service honours it only when that context is a spawn: the label is stored on the child row without the claim. The flag lives in the server-side creation context and is never read from request arguments, so `sessions.create` from a client, `sessions.patch` and `/name` keep their uniqueness check. ## Evidence - Executor test: a labeled worker spawn sends `sessions.create` with label "r1" and a spawn creation marked `unclaimedLabel`. It fails on main. - Handler test through the real `sessions.create`: two parents each spawn an r1 child and each resolves its own child with `sessions.resolve` scoped by `spawnedBy`; an unscoped resolve returns "Multiple sessions found", and a plain `sessions.create` with label r1 is still refused. Without the flag, or with the flag on a creation that is not a spawn, the label is claimed; a request that sends `unclaimedLabel` is rejected by the schema. Dropping the service change, or its spawn check, makes it fail. - Related session creation, resolve, patch, executor, visible spawn and spawn session-patch suites pass. oxlint, oxfmt and tsgo core are clean. - Local Gateway plus an `openclaw connect --session-host` worker with its own HOME, TMPDIR, state dir and workspace, gpt-4.1: two coordinators in a row, each spawning r1, r2 and r3. On main the second got "label already in use" for all three; with this change both got all three, and each coordinator's r1 resolved to its own child. - On OpenClaw Enterprise (runtime 35d714e), review-wait without a suffix fails on main with `label already in use: fast` and `slow`; every earlier run in the sidebar needed its own suffix (`fast-7`, `slow-d1`): With this change, two new sessions in a row (clear-lobster, then keen-prawn) each spawned `fast`, `slow` and `medium`, with no label error in the gateway log. In each run one child then failed to start for an unrelated reason, the device worker being at capacity ("all worker slots in use"); in keen-prawn that is `slow`, while `fast` and `medium` completed: Child worktrees from the gateway log, one group per coordinator (UTC): ``` $ jq -Rr 'fromjson? | select(.worktreePath) | "\(.time[11:19]) \(.worktreePath | split("/worktrees/")[1])"' gateway.log | grep -E '/(fast|slow|medium)-' 14:08:01 4a10b9376013d9dd/fast-528ef7 14:08:04 4a10b9376013d9dd/slow-d59672 14:08:08 4a10b9376013d9dd/medium-ee57fc 14:10:16 e6370d9404a6c199/fast-2d2ebc 14:10:19 e6370d9404a6c199/medium-78ba96 14:10:22 e6370d9404a6c199/slow-db8acb $ grep -c 'label already in use' gateway.log 0 ``` ## What this does not cover [1] Once a label repeats, a lookup by label alone is ambiguous:`sessions.resolve` returns "Multiple sessions found" instead of picking one. Hidden children already behave this way. Scoping by `spawnedBy` finds a parent's own child. Is failing closed here what you want, or should an unscoped lookup pick one, for example the newest child? [2] Visible spawns on the Gateway itself still claim the label. A Gateway agent can spawn hidden, which is the default; a worker cannot. Should every visible spawn treat its label as a task title, the way hidden spawns do? If so, the same flag fits there and I can send it as a follow-up. I'm happy to work on any follow-up you prefer. I'd still like to merge this one if possible, because it is blocking the RFE Creator port today. Related: #205476 (found while testing it, merged by @obviyus), #113950, #113331. cc @sallyom

prs.title: fix(agents): accept inert completion source-reply arguments
prs.body:
Closes #204016

Thanks @Unayung for the detailed reproduction.

## What Problem This Solves

A completion source reply is pinned to `action: "send"` and to the conversation that produced the turn, so most message-tool arguments carry no authority there. The policy rejected every argument outside a small allowlist, including values that cannot change the send: `targets: []`, `channelIds: []`, `dryRun: false`, `bestEffort: true`, `media: ""`, `attachments: []`, and `presentation: { title: "", blocks: [] }`.

Models that emit the full optional parameter set on every call (strict tool schemas) therefore got the same denial no matter how they retried. The retry loop ended as `repeated_tool_error` and the user never received the answer.

## User Impact

A completion reply now goes out when the model fills optional parameters with empty or default values. Values that carry content, routing, or a non-default delivery intent are still denied with the same policy error: non-empty targets, an enabled `dryRun`, `bestEffort: false` (required durable delivery), unknown flags, and presentation content.

## Why This Change Was Made

`isInertSourceReplyArgumentValue` proves a value empty: `undefined`, `null`, `""`, `false`, an empty array, or a plain object whose own values are all inert. Class instances, numbers, functions, and non-empty strings stay meaningful, and nesting past 16 levels fails closed instead of risking the call stack. Booleans also need the argument name: `false` is a no-op only for flags that default to false (`dryRun`, `silent`, `asVoice`, `asVideoNote`, `gifPlayback`, ...), while `bestEffort: false` is a real durable-delivery request and `bestEffort: true` is its default.

Accepted inert keys are then deleted from the tool's shallow dispatch copy. That deletion matters because downstream code treats presence as intent: an own `targets: []` sets `hasExplicitTargets` and suppresses implicit current-conversation routing, so tolerating the key without dropping it would still fail the send. Allowlisted content (`media`, `attachments`) stays.

## Evidence

New `src/agents/tools/message-tool-source-policy.test.ts` covers inert vs meaningful values, name-aware flag defaults, the nesting bound, and deletion of accepted keys. `message-tool.source-reply.test.ts` adds an integration case that dispatches with `targets`, `channelIds`, `dryRun`, `bestEffort`, and an empty `presentation`, then asserts none of the routing keys reach `runMessageAction`.

```
CI=1 ./node_modules/.bin/vitest run src/agents/tools/message-tool-source-policy.test.ts src/agents/tools/message-tool.source-reply.test.ts src/agents/tools/message-tool.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
  Test Files  3 passed (3)
  Tests       178 passed (178)
```

Formatting, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` are clean. Not exercised: a live model repeating the call against a real channel; the regression is covered at the policy and dispatch boundary named in the report.

## Merge danger

Two-way door: a revert restores the strict allowlist. No configuration, schema, or stored state changes; one new test file plus the policy module and one integration test.


## Real behavior proof

Head `05e40fbe25818221a58b9c04d028150af6aa0216`; base `c22b00d62e45283be53b7b88579b821e42dea4ca` (PR parent).

### Setup

- Isolated QA Lab run from this checkout: fresh temp HOME, config, state, and workspace per run; loopback Gateway on an ephemeral, non-default port; token auth (`auth=token` in the Gateway log); no external credentials or channels.
- Real: Gateway process, agent runtime, native subagent spawn and completion announce turn (`announce:v1:*`), `enforceSourceReplyOnlyMessageAction`, message tool dispatch, qa-channel plugin and QA bus, session transcript, Gateway logs.
- Stubbed: model is the repo's `mock-openai/gpt-5.6-luna` QA fixture. Channel transport is the synthetic `qa-channel` plugin.
- Harness-only, identical on both commits: a local QA scenario and a mock-provider edit (`extensions/qa-lab/src/providers/mock-openai/server.ts`) that adds the inert arguments to the scripted completion send. No product code changed.
- The real inbound DM starts the existing `silent` completion case. The native child completes empty; the completion announce turn calls `message` with:

  ```json
  {"action":"send","message":"QA-SUBAGENT-TERMINAL-SILENT-REPRESENTED","targets":[],"channelIds":[],"dryRun":false,"bestEffort":true,"presentation":{"title":"","blocks":[]}}
  ```

Commands (Node 24.22.1; run from the repo root; output dirs are repo-relative):

```bash
git switch --detach 05e40fbe25818221a58b9c04d028150af6aa0216
pnpm openclaw qa suite --provider-mode mock-openai --scenario zz-inert-completion-source-reply --output-dir .artifacts/qa-proof/head --concurrency 1

git switch --detach c22b00d62e45283be53b7b88579b821e42dea4ca
pnpm openclaw qa suite --provider-mode mock-openai --scenario zz-inert-completion-source-reply --output-dir .artifacts/qa-proof/base --concurrency 1 --allow-failures
```

### Head: completion send delivered to the originating conversation

- Suite: `Passed: 1`, `Failed: 0`.
- The completion model request carried the inert arguments:

  ```json
  {"requestKind":"tool-continuation","plannedToolName":"message","plannedToolArgs":{"action":"send","message":"QA-SUBAGENT-TERMINAL-SILENT-REPRESENTED","targets":[],"channelIds":[],"dryRun":false,"bestEffort":true,"presentation":{"title":"","blocks":[]}}}
  ```

- Message tool result (redacted): delivered to the same synthetic DM `terminal-inert-<id>`, with `"messageDelivery":{"partialDelivery":false,"status":"settled","sourceReplyDelivered":true}`.
- QA bus outbound rows for that DM: `Worker started.` then `QA-SUBAGENT-TERMINAL-SILENT-REPRESENTED`.
- Session transcript: `successfulToolCallCounts.message: 1`.
- Native subagent run: `execution.status: terminal`, `outcome.status: ok`, `delivery.status: delivered`.

### Base: same call denied before delivery

- Suite: `Passed: 0`, `Failed: 1`.
- Same completion model request and same inert arguments.
- Message tool result: `{"status":"error","tool":"message","error":"Completion source replies cannot use the \"targets\" argument."}`
- Gateway log: `[tools] message failed: MessageActionDeniedError: Completion source replies cannot use the "targets" argument.`
- QA bus outbound for that DM: only `Worker started.`; the completion marker is absent.
- Session transcript: `assistantToolCallCounts.message: 1`; `successfulToolCallCounts` has no `message`.

### Result

- Head: 1/1 passed; the completion send reached the originating conversation exactly once and the message tool recorded `sourceReplyDelivered: true`.
- Base: 0/1 passed; the identical call was denied before dispatch on `targets`.
- Limitation: the shipped path does not emit the post-policy argument map. The head evidence is the real dispatch outcome (settled source-reply delivery to the same conversation); the base evidence is the real pre-dispatch denial. Deletion of accepted keys is asserted by the policy and dispatch tests in this PR. Removing `targets: []` is also required for this send to route: an own `targets` property suppresses implicit current-conversation routing.

prs.title: fix: make the macOS local TTS example produce audio
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Following the "Local CLI" TTS example on macOS produces no audio at all. `say -o <OutputPath>` exits 1 with `Opening output file failed: fmt?` when the path has a `.wav` extension, unless a data format is passed explicitly, so every spoken reply fails until the user works out the missing flag.

Closes #206031

## User Impact

Copying the example now yields a working zero-key local TTS setup on macOS: the provider gets a RIFF/WAVE file that matches the example's `outputFormat: "wav"`. No other engine example changes, and no configuration keys change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add `--data-format=LEI16@22050` to the documented `say` arguments. `say` otherwise writes its default (AIFF) encoding and refuses a `.wav` destination, so the documented flag is the smallest change that makes the published example runnable as written.

## Evidence

Base (the currently documented arguments), exercised through the real provider path on macOS 15.7.4:

```
$ openclaw infer tts convert --text hello --output out.wav --local
TTS conversion failed: tts-local-cli: CLI TTS exit 1: Opening output file failed: fmt?
{"ok": false, "error": {"type": "cli_error", ...}}
$ ls out.wav
ls: out.wav: No such file or directory
```

With this change applied to the same config:

```
$ openclaw infer tts convert --text hello --output out.wav --local
... "outcome": "success", "reasonCode": "success" ...
"outputs": [ { "path": ".../out.wav", "format": "wav", "voiceCompatible": false } ]
$ file out.wav
out.wav: RIFF (little-endian) data, WAVE audio      # 23,348 bytes
```

Raw command confirmation: `say -o out.wav "hello"` exits 1 with `Opening output file failed: fmt?`; `say -o out.wav --data-format=LEI16@22050 "hello"` exits 0 and writes a RIFF/WAVE file.

Checks run on this branch: `pnpm format:docs:check` (clean, 1446 files), `pnpm lint:docs` (0 issues), `pnpm docs:check-mdx` (passed), `pnpm docs:check-links` (0 broken links), `pnpm docs:check-config-examples` (passed).

Not covered: the other local-engine examples (espeak, piper) were not executed on macOS, so this PR leaves them untouched.

prs.title: fix: post Discord voice replies as text when speech output fails
prs.body:
Closes #206037

Thanks @anmol0b for tracing the two terminal branches.

## What Problem This Solves

In Discord voice `stt-tts` mode, the agent turn runs with `deliver: false`, so the voice handler is the only thing that can return the answer. When speech synthesis fails, or the synthesized audio fails to play, the handler logs a warning and drops the completed reply. The user hears nothing and sees nothing, while the answer sits in session history.

## User Impact

A completed reply that cannot be spoken is now posted once as text in the voice channel's text chat. The normal spoken path, empty replies, and sessions that have already stopped behave as before. If the text fallback itself fails, the existing warning is extended with the reason and the voice loop keeps running.

## Why This Change Was Made

The realtime voice modes already solve this with a text fallback that sends through `sendMessageDiscord`; batch mode had no equivalent. The fallback here uses the same sender and the same `channel:<id>` target, guarded by the conversation-currency check and by the session lifecycle so a reply that settles after leave is not posted late. Synthesis failure and playback failure are separate terminal branches for a single reply, so only one of them can send. Playback keeps rethrowing so the playback queue still records the original failure.

## Evidence

A new regression file, `extensions/discord/src/voice/batch-text-fallback.test.ts`, drives the real voice receive path with the Discord send mocked and covers:

- Synthesis failure posts the reply once to `channel:1001` and never starts playback.
- Playback rejection posts the reply once and still logs `discord voice: playback failed: …`.
- A successful synthesis posts no text.
- An empty reply posts no text.
- A failed fallback send is logged without escaping the voice loop.

```
CI=1 ./node_modules/.bin/vitest run extensions/discord/src/voice/batch-text-fallback.test.ts extensions/discord/src/voice/segment.test.ts extensions/discord/src/voice/realtime-text-fallback.test.ts extensions/discord/src/voice/transcripts-conversation.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
  Test Files  4 passed (4)
  Tests       51 passed (51)
```

Formatting, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` are clean. Not exercised: a live Discord voice channel with a failing TTS provider; the change sits on the source-proven failure branches named in the report.

## Merge danger

Two-way door: a revert restores the warning-only behavior. No configuration, schema, or stored state changes; the new test file is the only addition outside the voice segment handler.

prs.title: fix(codex): cold web-search support verdicts no longer rotate bound threads
prs.body:
Closes #174676

## What Problem This Solves
Fixes: a Codex conversation's native thread is replaced — re-sending its full selected history — on the second turn after a Gateway cold start, because turn 1 recorded the web-search policy from a cold capability probe.

## User Impact
Conversations that start right after a Gateway start keep their native thread and prompt context. A cold "unsupported" capability read no longer forces a full history re-send once the provider's web-search support resolves (the issue measured ~1.2M characters re-injected on a lossless session).

## Why This Change Was Made
A cold app-server can answer `modelProvider/capabilities/read` before its model metadata hydrates, producing a definitive-looking "unsupported" verdict. The lifecycle persisted that verdict's disabled thread config as the binding's authoritative web-search fingerprint, so the first informed turn counted the change as a persistent policy change and rotated the thread.

The preflight now also computes the fingerprint an uninformed ("unknown") plan produces under the same config. When a binding's stored fingerprint equals that uninformed shape and the current plan is informed, the lifecycle adopts the informed fingerprint on the existing thread instead of replacing it. Genuine policy edits (allowed domains, provider opt-outs, persistent denial) move the plan away from the uninformed shape and still rotate as before; a first turn under an "unknown" verdict already keeps a provisional binding and is untouched.

The stored fingerprint alone cannot prove the plan was uninformed: an explicit `tools.web.search.enabled=false` turn writes the same disabled shape. The binding now also records whether the durable policy requested search (`webSearchRequested`, taken from `persistentWebSearchAllowed` with the effective value as fallback, so capability filtering such as domain-restricted management does not look like a denial). Cold-support settlement requires `webSearchRequested: true`, so re-enabling an explicitly disabled search remains a policy transition that rotates; bindings written before this field keep rotating exactly as before.

## Evidence
- Regression in `thread-lifecycle-web-search.test-support.ts` (registered from the binding suite): turn 1 under `nativeProviderWebSearchSupport: "unsupported"` persists the disabled fingerprint; turn 2 under `"supported"` keeps `thread-1` with exactly one `thread/start`. Fails on base — the thread is replaced via the "web search config changed" rotation named in the issue — and passes with this change.
- Policy-transition regression: turn 1 persists an explicit denial (`webSearchRequested: false`, disabled fingerprint); turn 2 enables search with a supported verdict and rotates to `thread-2` with two `thread/start` calls. This is the case the earlier revision misclassified as cold settlement.
- The branch is rebased on current `main`; both regressions and the 4 neighboring search cases pass (6/6 `-t search`, plus the cold-verdict case), and the new test-line allocation `174676-codex-web-search.txt` (63 lines) is the exact net growth.
- Neighbors stay green: 5/5 `search`-filtered cases in `thread-lifecycle.binding.test.ts` (including the existing unknown-support preservation case) and 8/8 in `thread-lifecycle.assignment-rotation.test.ts`, run with `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` on Node 24.19.
- Not run locally: full extension suite and project typecheck (CI covers).

prs.title: fix(browser): report a crashed tab instead of a timeout
prs.body:
Related: #194667

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a tab whose renderer process dies keeps being treated as a normal page, so `snapshot` waits for its full timeout and fails with a generic timeout plus the "browser is currently unavailable" retry hint, while `screenshot`/`navigate` surface raw Playwright text (`page.screenshot: Target crashed`). The agent is told the whole browser is unavailable even though only that tab is dead, and retries the dead target instead of opening a new tab.

## User Impact

User impact: every action on a crashed tab now fails at once with `tab crashed (renderer exited); open the URL in a new tab and retry` (HTTP 409, no retry hint), and the dead tab can still be removed with `browser close`.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The per-page state records Playwright's `crash` event, and page resolution refuses a target whose renderer already died instead of letting the operation run against it.
- Crash facts are also keyed by `cdpUrl + targetId`, so a replacement `Page` object for the same target remains refused after reconnect or re-enumeration.
- Target identity is independent of document-scoped role refs, so main-frame navigation cannot erase a later crash report.
- Batch resolution admits the target for per-child admission. Close-only batches retain the crash exemption needed for cleanup, while every non-close child still refuses the dead renderer with the typed conflict.
- A crash raised during a batch child is rethrown through the existing route mapper instead of becoming a raw child-result string, and later children stop even with `stopOnError=false`.
- Native text insertion preserves the crash classification before its sanitizing fallback; ordinary insertion failures still drop the original error and cannot expose pasted text through an error cause. The intentional suppression is recorded in the repository's explicit production-suppression allowlist.
- Every close path skips the crash assertion because removing the dead tab is the recovery action recommended by the error.
- Playwright's raw crash errors are normalized before matching: only Playwright's own framing maps, including page/locator and keyboard/mouse APIs, after comparing the first line with trailing whitespace and browser logs removed.

The follow-up regression uses the real `getPageForTargetId` and real `closePageViaPlaywright`, rather than copying crash admission into a mock resolver. `Related` is intentional: tab-list crash markers remain a separate follow-up.

## Evidence

Real managed Chrome 138 profile, renderer killed with CDP `Page.crash` on `http://127.0.0.1:18080/`:

| action | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `browser snapshot` | 17.0 s, `page.ariaSnapshot: Target crashed` | 6.7 s total, explicit tab-recovery message |
| `browser navigate` | raw `Target crashed` | same explicit message |
| `browser screenshot` | raw `Target crashed` | same explicit message |
| `browser close` | n/a | `{"ok": true}`, tab removed |
| healthy-tab snapshot (control) | 7.0 s | 7.0 s |

The after timings include ~6.5 s of CLI startup; the crashed-tab request itself returns as fast as a healthy one.

Regression coverage:

- With the previous parent-only batch admission, the real-resolver close-only regression fails with `BrowserTabCrashedError`; the click regression records `[false]` instead of `[true, undefined]`. Production was restored after the red proof.
- The close-only batch now crosses the real resolver and real close helper, closes the crashed page, and records `[true, true]`: the parent and close helper both retain the exemption.
- The click batch rejects `BrowserTabCrashedError` without clicking and records `[true, undefined]`, proving that the child performs its own refusal after the parent admits the batch.
- The in-flight batch regression returned an unmapped child result before the fix; it now maps the propagated crash to HTTP 409 and proves a later hover is not called with `stopOnError=false`.
- The native-insertion regression returned the sanitized ordinary paste failure before the fix; it now rejects `BrowserTabCrashedError`. The existing synthetic-password control still proves that ordinary Playwright insertion failures expose neither the text nor its original error cause.
- Keyboard/mouse crash prefixes map to the same 409, while page-script errors containing `Target crashed` and ordinary target-close errors retain their existing classification.
- `pw-session-state.crash.test.ts` also covers crash identity after navigation clears role refs and replacement `Page` objects for the same target.
- Focused errors + batch suites after the final fixes: **26/26 tests passed**, including **20/20** batch tests and the ordinary paste-sanitization control.
- Final `pnpm test:extension browser` in the qualified Node 24 container with Docker init: **2994 passed, 116 skipped** in the browser config and **158 passed** in the database-workers config; exit 0.
- `oxfmt --check`: clean. Focused production syntax lint and type-aware lint for the changed suppression inventory: 0 warnings/errors. Mock-export ratchet: **6359** grandfathered factories after exactly two retired entries were removed. Test-line ratchet: **6579642, ceiling 6579643, slack 1**, with exact net regression allocation **276** and no shared-scalar increase.
- **Final autoreview (Claude engine), P0–P2**, from merge-base `1cba5e993` through the working tree later committed as `77f79a52f0fe192cabd74323aac11da40ea2b0a4`: one complete pass, machine status **`scoped-clean`**, with no accepted/actionable findings. The reviewer did not execute tests; the focused and full-lane results above are separate local proof.

Type validation: the repository's exact `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/extensions-test.tsbuildinfo` command passed in a `node:24-bookworm` container after the final edits. The host could not execute the pinned `tsrs` binary because its GLIBC is too old; the container supplied the required runtime without changing dependencies or bypassing the check. Direct `tsc` without built SDK declarations was not used as a substitute. No second managed Chrome run is claimed for the final targeted in-flight batch/insertText fixes; their added proof is through the production owners and existing route mapper.

## Known boundaries

- `action=tabs` still lists a crashed tab as a normal page; marking it is a follow-up that needs a target-scoped crash registry outside the live connection.
- A crash that happens before this process registers the listener (fresh attach to an already-crashed external target) is not retro-detected.
- Chrome MCP (`existing-session`) profiles never resolve a Playwright `Page`, so they get the message mapping only.


### Real Behavior Proof (Batch & Native Insertion on Managed Chromium 156)

Executed against a real headless Chromium (`Chrome/156.0.8078.73`) over a local loopback CDP endpoint through shipped `executeActViaPlaywright` + `toBrowserErrorResponse`:

1. **Healthy tab control** (`batch` with `stopOnError: false` containing `click` -> `insertText("healthy-input")` -> `click`): succeeded (`results=[true,true,true]`, `boxValue="healthy-input"`, `clickCount=1`).
2. **Permissive batch mid-run tab crash** (`batch` with `stopOnError: false`, `Page.crash` triggered mid-step 1 before step 2 `click #b2`): stopped before step 2, threw `page.waitForTimeout: Page crashed`, classified by `isBrowserTabCrashedError=true`, mapped to **HTTP 409** `"tab crashed (renderer exited); open the URL in a new tab and retry"`.
3. **Native insertion (`insertText`) on crashed tab**: threw `BrowserTabCrashedError` (`instanceof=true`), mapped to **HTTP 409** `"tab crashed (renderer exited); open the URL in a new tab and retry"`, with `leaksText=false` (inserted token not echoed in error message).

```text
[repro] Chromium started: Chrome/156.0.8078.73
[1. healthy-control] results=[true,true,true] boxValue="healthy-input" clickCount=1
[2. permissive-batch-midrun-crash] isBrowserTabCrashedError=true status=409 body="tab crashed (renderer exited); open the URL in a new tab and retry" raw="page.waitForTimeout: Page crashed"
[3. native-insertion-crashed-tab] isBrowserTabCrashedError=false instanceof=true status=409 leaksText=false body="tab crashed (renderer exited); open the URL in a new tab and retry"
```

prs.title: improve: reduce memory when an agent database opens
prs.body:
## Problem

Opening an agent database can load the host-side SQLite worker broker into the database worker itself. The agent-deletion journal needs one synchronous provenance deletion, which it previously imported through the host-facing reader and writer. This was a separate follow-up identified during the [transcript worker investigation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/177242).

## User Impact

A shared Gateway worker does less work when opening an agent database. Agent deletion still removes creation provenance only when the matching journal operation completes and its transaction commits. Existing agent databases, configuration and update behavior use the same interfaces.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing provenance kernel already owns synchronous operations on an admitted database handle. The journal now imports the deletion there. It uses the same SQL, normalization, connection and staged publication. The host continues to own asynchronous provenance recording. The product change removes seven lines overall.

## Evidence

- On Linux x64 with Node 24.22.1, both variants used the normal `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` package build on the same guest. The packaged preparation API opened a seeded agent database under the lean profile. The product worker registry and the isolate's own thread ID identified the physical shared host before teardown. [Testbox allocation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45946083209)
- V8 execution coverage on that host went from 541 to 539 package files. Their emitted code totaled 5,637,597 bytes before and 5,579,272 after. The candidate stopped evaluating the host broker and facade. The in-database provenance kernel remained available.
- Across three fresh heap samples per variant, median physical V8 heap went from 61.41 to 60.65 MiB. Median used heap went from 41.21 to 40.39 MiB. Individual ranges overlap. These are measurements of one worker at database admission.
- The broker import regression failed on stock. All 43 tests in the five affected and neighboring suites passed on the candidate. They cover journal ownership, rollback, committed deletion publication, a second database containing the same agent ID, and agent database registration.
- The package and transaction comparison used `d95d852e054f`. The final commit retains the same product and test files, with two inventory totals reconciled over a concurrent change. The stock full inventory already differed from its tracked snapshot. The generator measured one fewer worker-access file and the same call count, and the tracked update preserves that scoped delta. The repository SQLite worker ratchet passed against that stock revision.
- Final committed-range autoreview found no actionable findings.

prs.title: fix: skip extra approval for comments on the session PR
prs.body:
Closes #206119

## What Problem This Solves

Agents need a separate confirmation to comment on the PR their current session is already working on, even though creating that PR needs no such confirmation. For comments on other targets, Codex can cancel the required five-minute approval after only 90 seconds.

## User Impact

Comments on the session's selected or currently published PR post without another approval. Comments on other issues or PRs in the registered repository still require approval of the exact target, posting account and text, and retain their full five-minute lifetime. The tool still cannot choose another repository. No configuration change is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

I use the existing session PR association, or its current publication receipt when there is no selected PR, with an exact host/repository/PR match. The exception does not cover every PR authored by the selected account. Session/project access, publisher identity checks, comment outcome logging and unconfirmed-write handling stay intact.

I also reuse the existing `getExecutionTimeoutMs` contract. The GitHub tool declares its ten-minute dispatch budget for comment creation, and Codex honors declared tool budgets with completion grace. Parent cancellation and approval expiry stay in force for other targets.

I ran pr-simplify without introducing another setting, state store or permission mechanism. Against the base, production changes are +75/-39 lines and tests are +122/-1 lines, plus the documentation update. The regression shares the existing publication fixture and covers both supported sources of the session PR.

## Evidence

### Live Gateway verification at `9419697b9aa8c0547bfbaaf969a8221b24ac8379`

An isolated OpenClaw Gateway with a real model exercised all three cases on November 27, 2026 UTC.

- **Selected PR:** The model posted one GitHub comment on the session's selected PR. The Gateway issued zero approval requests.
- **PR published by the session:** The model posted one GitHub comment on the PR identified by the session's publication receipt. The Gateway issued zero approval requests.
- **Different target:** The Gateway issued one approval request when the selected-PR session targeted a different PR in the same repository. GitHub showed zero matching comments while approval was pending and exactly one after the operator chose **Allow once**.

GitHub readback confirmed the posting account and one comment per case, with zero duplicate writes.

### Automated checks

For the exemption, both new regressions failed without the change. AWS VM checks passed 131 focused tests across the publication action, comment, tool-description and Codex watchdog consumers. Formatting, targeted lint, core and test typechecks passed. The checks cover the session's published and selected PRs, other-target consent, and host/repository mismatches. GitHub transport is mocked in these regressions; they are not live-model proof.

Local autoreview remains unavailable because the selected Codex installation cannot execute inside its read-only review sandbox. I did not relax the sandbox.

### Earlier live proof of the retained watchdog fix

I’m including the redacted real-Gateway Codex verification supplied by @daniel-lxs for head `9e9ec40`:

```text
Head 9e9ec40 | Codex harness | github_publish.create_comment | approval TTL 300000 ms
Allow  | prior run | pending at 96100 ms | allowed | confirmed GitHub comments=1
Deny   | pending at 96027 ms | plugin.approval.resolve accepted | denied/user at 96073 ms | resolver=runtime
Expiry | pending at 96009 ms | no decision submitted | expired/timeout at 300002 ms | resolver=system
Stop   | pending at 96008 ms | chat.abort accepted (aborted=true) | cancelled/run-aborted at 96149 ms | resolver=system
Deny, Expiry, Stop | GitHub write attempts=0 | disposable PR comments 0 -> 0
```

- The reported plain-Gateway reproduction on main `36395007cf0` used a real model through Codex. The approval was system-cancelled after 89.998 seconds with 210 seconds remaining.
- I ran both focused files on an AWS VM with Node 24.22.1. Without the production fix, both regressions failed, including the exact `90000ms` watchdog result. With the fix, all **57 tests passed** across both files.
- The fake-clock watchdog regression completes after 310 seconds, past the approval lifetime, under the declared operation budget. The producer check protects the comment budget and unchanged readiness default.
- I verified the final file hashes against the VM-tested source. Formatting, targeted lint and the core typecheck passed with no warnings or errors.
- Local autoreview was unavailable: the installed Codex executable could not run inside its read-only review sandbox. I did not weaken that sandbox. I did not independently repeat the supplied live-model replay.


Cleanup: AWS test leases were released and prior proof scratch was removed. No Team Gateway configuration or consent setting was changed.

Contributor: Dan Riccio (@daniel-lxs).

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/task-roboclaw-comment-approval-timeout-s5518cecd)
