prs.body:
> [!NOTE]
> Draft for code-owner review. Not ready to land.

Co-authored by Vyctor Brzezowski (`vyctorbrzezowski`).

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with Vyctor Brzezowski](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/bfb77f08-1fd2-461f-ada5-4f3ff81fa044)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/ab752961-46e2-42cb-9b74-07a56df10671)
- [Implementation and verification (conflict and review fixes)](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/task-automations-cleanup-prs-sc663a40b)

## What Problem This Solves

Gmail Pub/Sub watches have their own start, reload, and shutdown paths in the Gateway. That makes them harder to maintain than other mail triggers, which use the standard plugin lifecycle. This draft moves watcher ownership first; it is not the complete Gmail cutover.

## User Impact

The bundled `gmail` plugin starts and renews the watcher. Existing `hooks.gmail` settings, HTTP mappings, `openclaw webhooks gmail` commands, and stored automations are unchanged. This slice does not rewrite, pause, or delete jobs, and adds no Doctor migration. If you restrict `plugins.allow`, include `gmail` for the Gateway-managed watcher; if plugins are disabled, the Gateway will not start it. Restart the Gateway after configuring the watcher for the first time so it loads the plugin. `OPENCLAW_SKIP_GMAIL_WATCHER=1` still opts out of Gateway startup.

## Why This Change Was Made

The plugin uses the existing scheduled service contract for startup, reload, and shutdown instead of a second Gateway lifecycle. The move exposes the shared process helpers needed to preserve executable lookup, Windows wrapper quoting, bounded diagnostics, and process-tree cleanup; it adds no Gmail-specific SDK API. The generated config inventory counts 24 additional standard plugin-entry fields for `gmail`; this slice adds no Gmail settings and leaves the core and channel counts unchanged.

Still to do before landing the full cutover: move the persisted settings and mapping defaults, add Doctor migration and upgrade proof (including restrictive plugin policy), remove the Gmail-specific model/reasoning precedence and startup model check, and move CLI registration and Gog Doctor diagnostics out of core. Likely sibling overlap is in Gateway reload, automation model selection, Doctor migrations, and generated config/plugin inventories. This slice does not change the automation protocol, agent tool, or editor.

## Evidence

- I merged main at `fc25865d99bd0166efbe6f70d93df979e68e19ac`, retaining both SDK documentation sections and regenerating the config/plugin inventories. No rebase or force-push.
- I reproduced the port regression before fixing it: Gmail selected a service-only reload for `gateway.port`. The regression now passes, preserving the core Gateway restart policy from #138556 and hot reloads for hook settings. Implementation tests and private mocks now live with the plugin.
- I ran 542 focused tests across 20 files locally, without a VM, in 169.23 seconds. They cover Gateway reload/startup/shutdown, hook mapping, Gmail setup, CLI/Doctor and the relocated suites. The fake-Gog integration exercised real spawning, child-only token transport and process-tree cleanup, not live Google delivery.
- Core typecheck, lint, format, all three plugin boundaries, mock-export ratchet and generated inventories passed. The full build emitted Gmail entrypoints and exited 0, with three Control UI budget violations: largest CSS gzip, chat boot JS requests and chat boot JS gzip. Budgets were not relaxed.
- The pr-simplify pass retained one lifecycle owner and removed the plugin's direct normalization dependency in favor of existing SDK exports. Regeneration also removed an unrelated `optional` marker on `escape-string-regexp@4.0.0`, with no version changes. Against merged main: non-test +262/-235; tests +128/-500.
- Local P0-P1 autoreview was unavailable: its read-only sandbox preflight rejected the selected Codex installation. No assessment was produced, permissions were not broadened, and no hosted re-review was requested.

Still needed before landing: shipped-Gateway Gmail discovery/activation, hook reload, port rebinding and shutdown proof; live Gmail Pub/Sub forwarding; upgrades retaining settings and exercising disabled/restrictive plugin policies from v2026.11.5 and supported 9.x extended-stable/10.x sources. Final-head CI and completed independent review remain unverified. This stays a draft.

prs.title: feat(rapid-mlx): support local chat and memory embeddings
prs.body:
Related: #197555

## What Problem This Solves

Rapid-MLX users need a named setup and memory-search provider in OpenClaw.

## User Impact

User impact: choose **Rapid-MLX** during setup, discover local chat models, and use `rapid-mlx/<model-id>` or an explicitly served embedding model for memory search. Rapid-MLX is an open-source local LLM inference server for Apple Silicon, built on MLX.

## Why This Change Was Made

Follows the bundled oMLX provider in #173327, reusing OpenAI-compatible transports with optional authentication and a default URL of `http://localhost:8000/v1`. Includes provider and memory docs, navigation, generated inventories, tests, official app/onboarding icons, and an existing generic activity glyph. No new external dependencies or changes to oMLX.

## Evidence

The before capture uses the same shared build with the new Rapid-MLX plugin omitted; the after capture includes the provider and its official-site onboarding icon. Both images were inspected and contain no personal data.

![After: Rapid-MLX entry, official icon, and Connect server action](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raullenchai/openclaw/rapid-mlx-pr-assets/after.png)

The 1,050-line allocation preserves the existing provider's auth and embedding boundary coverage.

Reply with just the number.' --thinking off --json` returned `42` through Rapid-MLX. Direct streaming also returned `42` with usage metadata.

Live embeddings were not tested because the local Rapid-MLX server serves a chat model. Feature request: #197555.

## Verification (review follow-up)

prs.title: fix(ui): align offline shell terminal capability with CSP
prs.body:
Fixes #205656.

## What Problem This Solves

After the Control UI recovers from its cached offline shell, reconnecting to a Gateway with Terminal enabled can expose Terminal in a document whose CSP cannot compile WebAssembly. Ghostty then fails and its fallback asset requests can display a misleading 404.

## User Impact

Terminal stays disabled in the offline document until an existing config refresh can request a reload into a document with the appropriate CSP. Unsaved-work reload guards remain respected. Releasing a guard alone does **not** trigger a reload: a subsequent config refresh requests it once permitted. No configuration changes or migration are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The offline-shell producer now declares `data-openclaw-terminal-enabled="false"`, matching its strict CSP. This reuses the existing document-policy reconciliation and reload guard; it neither widens CSP nor adds another reload mechanism.

The regression uses the shared service-worker harness to install synthetic build assets, receive actual worker-generated HTML after a 503 navigation, and apply its attributes before importing config. It extends the existing reload-owner test instead of duplicating it, retaining the guarded transition and proving that an explicit later refresh requests exactly one reload. Existing navigation cases retain CSP/import-map and root/subpath coverage.

## Evidence

Verified against base `c7824fb4d2b0f11fd3e6e9740f30489dba150b76`:

- **Red before repair:** the changed suites failed in four expected cases: three missing-marker navigation assertions, and Terminal incorrectly becoming enabled while the reload guard blocked.
- **Green after repair:** `pnpm test ui/src/app/service-worker-cache.test.ts ui/src/app/document-reload-owners.test.ts ui/src/app/config.test.ts ui/src/app/vite-config-cache.node.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — **4 files, 71 tests passed**, runner shard wall time 2.62s. This independently observed count replaces the previously reported 72; the existing reload-owner case was expanded, not duplicated.
- Changed suites also ran separately with `pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`: service-worker cache, 52 tests, runner wall time 1.35s (Vitest 414ms); document reload owners, 1 test, runner wall time 1.58s (Vitest 713ms). Per-suite CI seconds were not extracted; the complete CI workflow finished successfully.
- `pnpm format:check ui/public/sw.js ui/src/app/service-worker-cache.test.ts ui/src/app/document-reload-owners.test.ts` — passed.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs ui/public/sw.js ui/src/app/service-worker-cache.test.ts ui/src/app/document-reload-owners.test.ts` — passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:ui`, `pnpm tsgo:test:ui`, and `git diff --check` — passed.
- `pnpm ui:build` — passed, including finalized compressed-sidecar verification. The emitted worker contains the Terminal-disabled marker and its offline CSP excludes `wasm-unsafe-eval`. The build's report-only performance step reported largest CSS gzip 58,659 B versus 58,315 B and chat boot JS 21 requests versus 20; this is not a passing performance-budget check.
- `pr-simplify` author pass: retained the existing producer, reload owner, and shared harness; no new production mechanism. Delta against base: production +2/-1 lines; tests +41/-9 lines. Test growth covers the actual offline HTML-to-config boundary rather than a hand-supplied capability marker.
- Bound Auto Review of the complete three-file local snapshot against the base above (verified tree-identical to published head `61c779b076f614b21a31cfaed50ea80f60546cc9`): `scoped-clean`, no findings at its default **P0-only** priority. **Verification gaps:** These are VM/jsdom boundary tests with synthetic network responses, not real-browser, Gateway, Ghostty-rendering, or PTY proof. No live reproduction of the fallback 404, local full Gateway build, or production-browser/Gateway/PTY acceptance proof is claimed. prs.title: fix(android): load cursor history without losing reading position
prs.body:
Related: #191596

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Android cannot browse earlier chat pages and can pull readers to a new remote prompt while they are reading history.

## User Impact

User impact: readers can load older messages, catch up with cursor deltas, and keep their reading position while live responses arrive. Confirmed reasoning-level changes now survive subsequent delta reconciliation, so later sends do not revert to the old history window's level.

Cursor resets and reconnects reopen the normal tail; pages outside that tail must be loaded again. Existing full-message expansion survives unchanged history updates, but its Compose-local fetched content can require **View all** again after Activity recreation. No Gateway contract, cache retention, schema, dependencies, or outbox retry policy changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The chat controller now owns cursor-backed history windows, validates complete delta envelopes before advancing their cursor, and uses the same canonical upsert for live message events and catch-up. Directional pages do not supply branch/run/outbox evidence. Snapshot-only Gateways keep their existing reads.

The reader distinguishes remote content from explicit local send intent, saves a stable row key and offset, and leaves **Jump to latest** in its existing header location. **Beginning of conversation** requires explicit `hasMore: false` coverage on a normal snapshot, or exhaustion of a successful advertised directional older-page read. Directional pages omit `hasMore`; missing cursors on bounded/legacy snapshots or cached views still do not prove completeness. Config changes force a normal history read because deltas omit default-model metadata.

## Evidence

### Current-main integration proof

The signed merge `d5c45f6f8d45` keeps @saariuslystoned’s pagination work on the original branch and incorporates main at `40d533668293`. It preserves reconnect, wake and pending-send handling alongside the history cursor checks.

The focused Android Gradle run passed all 10 `ChatControllerHistoryCursorTest` cases in each of the Play and third-party flavors. The two added cases exercise stale pages across reconnect and session switching, and older-page retries on the same route while the live tail remains visible.

The [existing unfolded Pixel recording](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191597#issuecomment-6758176947) covers scroll position. Fold recreation and the terminal-chat plus session-message sequence in [#199737](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/199737) remain unverified by these tests.

### Source identity and bounded repairs

- Current published head: `f703f9c03ba15664cecf477222fe159a4f37a2d6` on `openclaw/fast-crab`, updated on this same draft PR through native `github_publish` (publication receipt `8dd002c3-74a9-4ffc-accb-dea7bce2cc3d`). The published commit contains only the two-file thinking-level repair described below.
- Previous published/reviewed head: `cdc305f8add626cb6c5c9ff94a18bfec1bb90f51`; earlier reviewed head: `2ef1d3d0763c7f67955aad92f70db7c0edd088d6`. Original attachment base: `65dfe23a008b733fbdaf0dc79762149345f75d06`; managed guest source base/HEAD: `913f025cd15ba79d4002ad4e6db1fe2739ba8f8f`. The publisher appends remote commits without moving the guest HEAD; these are distinct identities.
- The original attachment SHA-256 was `d31ee6e735c3187415d811129aa246c712b48eb9b713c350dd07d0220afe9c1b`; its initial publication was `3376cb779d631ae7bc803d347d4fc027e22b40f9`. Those hashes identify earlier revisions, not this repaired candidate.
- Repair input: the [exact-head local verification](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191597#issuecomment-6593866579) and [downloadable evidence/provenance correction](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191597#issuecomment-6593999941). The evidence archive's 19 files were checked against its SHA-256/size manifest. That earlier archive's 3,789-test reference belongs to the initial revision; its `2ef1d3d` result is 172 targeted tests. The separate exact-head `cdc305f8add6` full-suite evidence is recorded below.
- Reset events now retire advertised cursor windows without skipping the existing session-settings publication path. Queued permission writes still observe the replacement physical session identity; snapshot-only metadata refreshes do not gain extra history reads.
- Display IDs remain distinct from canonical transcript entry IDs. Canonical reconciliation preserves display identity across cursor updates without admitting a display ID to a reaction write.
- Reader fixtures preserve the intended ownership contract: remote history does not force-follow; an explicit **Jump to latest** moves the reader; local send admission starts following; final-answer fixture rows and navigation through the reader owner exercise stable-position restoration. Existing session/permission and reader-position assertions were retained, with a negative remote-follow assertion added.
- Latest P2 repair: `parseHistory` uses the current top-level `thinkingLevel`, then the current `sessionInfo.thinkingLevel`, and no longer inherits that setting from `previousHistory`. If both are absent, the existing settings owner retains its confirmed value. Existing generation/pending-mutation guards and snapshot precedence are unchanged.
- The new `ChatControllerHistoryCursorTest.deltaRunReconciliationPreservesConfirmedThinkingLevel` regression completes a settings mutation before normal send-driven reconciliation, checks current/omitted/newer Gateway metadata, and asserts the next serialized `chat.send` thinking value.
- No new owner, schema, dependency, configuration option, permission policy, or queue-lane change. The earlier repair was nine files (+559/−339, mostly canonical Kotlin formatting). This follow-up is two files (+74/−1: production +2/−1, test +72), removing stale settings inheritance rather than adding another state owner. The complete local patch against the managed source base is 13 files (+1200/−53).

### Executed checks

The published two-file patch matches the locally tested and independently reviewed candidate. Linux x64, Eclipse Temurin `21.0.12.1+1-LTS`, worktree-local Android/Gradle/Robolectric caches.

This is a production-controller/outbox boundary test with scripted external Gateway I/O, not a live-device run.
- **Green:** canonical `:app:ktlintFormat`, then a separate `:app:ktlintCheck` plus targeted tests: **94/94 passed; 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped**. The combined check/test run reported **BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 54s**; app and test Kotlin compilation succeeded.

Command from `apps/android` (with worktree-local cache setup):

```sh
./gradlew --no-daemon --max-workers=2 :app:ktlintCheck :app:testThirdPartyDebugUnitTest \
```

prs.title: fix(plugins): read plugin policy through the canonical enable owner
prs.body:
Closes #205672

## What Problem This Solves

Running `openclaw doctor` with `plugins.allow: []` and an enabled Codex entry silently drops the personal Codex asset reminder, the `/tools` inventory notice tells operators to add `browser` to `plugins.allow` even when the browser plugin was disabled somewhere else entirely, and the OpenShell workspace binding ignores a padded denylist entry and enables File Transfer against the operator's policy.

- Problem: three call sites decided plugin enablement by hand instead of asking the existing policy owner, so they disagreed with what actually loads. The doctor scan treated any `allow` array as authoritative and never consulted `entries`, so an empty allowlist (which restricts nothing, as established in #191708) turned the scan off. The `/tools` notice blamed `plugins.allow` for every missing browser and produced no notice at all when the plugin was denylisted. The OpenShell workspace binding compared raw ids in `allow`/`deny`/`entries`, so `" File-Transfer "` never matched the denylist and the binding enabled File Transfer anyway.
- Solution: each site now normalizes with `normalizePluginsConfig` and asks `resolveEffectiveEnableState` for the decision, which returns both `enabled` and the reason (`plugins disabled` / `blocked by denylist` / `disabled in config` / `not in allowlist`). The notice now names that reason and only suggests editing `plugins.allow` when the allowlist is actually the cause.
- What changed: `extensions/openshell/src/worker-workspace.ts`, `src/commands/doctor/shared/codex-native-assets.ts` and `src/agents/tools-effective-inventory.ts` replace their hand-rolled checks with the shared owner; the new scenarios are folded into three existing test cases (net test line delta -1).
- What did NOT change: the decision order, empty-allowlist semantics and every other rule still live in `resolveEffectiveEnableState`; no new option, schema, or config surface was added, and the two notices keep their existing ids and severities.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Best fix: route all three call sites through the single existing owner (`normalizePluginsConfig` + `resolveEffectiveEnableState`) rather than teaching each site the policy rules again. The owner already encodes the order deny -> entry -> allowlist and the empty-allowlist rule, and the repo already uses it this way from `extensions/browser/src/plugin-enabled.ts` and `extensions/codex/index.ts`, so this removes duplicated policy instead of adding a fourth variant.
- Alternative(s): patching each site locally (add an `allow.length > 0` guard, add a deny check, normalize the ids inline) was rejected because it leaves three copies of the same policy that can drift again; writing a new shared helper for these three callers was rejected because the owner already exists.
- Risk: the doctor scan and the OpenShell gate now consult the bundled default (`enabledByDefault`) as well as the config, so a Codex config block or an explicit allowlist entry counts as opt-in even with an empty allowlist. That matches what the Codex plugin itself gates on, and the widest supported case (no `plugins` section at all) still skips the scan, as before. The notice's accessory sentence changed for non-allowlist causes, so any doc that quoted the old sentence needs a look.

## User Impact

Operators who keep an empty `plugins.allow` now still see the personal Codex asset reminder, and when the browser tool is missing the reason reported matches the reason the plugin is actually off. Following that advice no longer means widening plugin policy for a plugin that was disabled on purpose. An operator who denylisted File Transfer (even with padded whitespace in the id) no longer gets it silently re-enabled by an OpenShell workspace binding.

## Evidence

Every cell below states its full `plugins` input. Doctor cells share one `HOME` fixture containing two personal skills (`.codex/skills/tweet-helper/SKILL.md` and `.agents/skills/agent-helper/SKILL.md`); the count is `grep -c 'Personal Codex CLI assets found'` on `doctor --non-interactive` output. Every `tools.effective` cell also has `browser: { enabled: true }` in the config; the notice column quotes the `browser-plugin-not-allowed` message.

| Case | Full `plugins` input | Before (base `1342a4e`) | After (head `eb5e466`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| doctor, empty allow + enabled entry | `{"allow":[],"entries":{"codex":{"enabled":true}}}` | 0 asset lines | 1 line, `2 skills` |
| doctor, enabled entry, no allow key (control) | `{"entries":{"codex":{"enabled":true}}}` | 1 line, `2 skills` | 1 line, `2 skills` |
| doctor, padded allow id (control) | `{"allow":[" CODEX "]}` | 1 line, `2 skills` | 1 line, `2 skills` |
| doctor, padded deny id (control) | `{"allow":[],"deny":[" Codex "]}` | 0 | 0 |
| doctor, allowlist without codex (control) | `{"allow":["slack"]}` | 0 | 0 |
| doctor, no plugins section (control) | (key absent) | 0 | 0 |
| tools.effective, entry disabled | `{"allow":[],"entries":{"browser":{"enabled":false}}}` | `plugins.allow does not include browser` | `disabled in config` |
| tools.effective, plugins globally disabled | `{"enabled":false,"allow":[]}` | `plugins.allow does not include browser` | `plugins disabled` |
| tools.effective, denylisted | `{"deny":["browser"]}` | no notice at all | `blocked by denylist` |
| tools.effective, browser enabled (control) | `{"entries":{"browser":{"enabled":true}}}` | no notice | no notice |
| tools.effective, empty allow only (control) | `{"allow":[]}` | no notice | no notice |
| tools.effective, other allow + entry on (control) | `{"allow":["slack"],"entries":{"browser":{"enabled":true}}}` | no notice | no notice |

| Case | Before (base `1342a4e`) | After (head `eb5e466`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| openshell worker configure, `plugins.deny: [" File-Transfer "]` + agent workspace binding | exit 0; config rewritten with File Transfer enabled and the workspace binding applied | exit 1; refusal message; config file byte-identical |
| upgrade, latest stable -> head, same state dir, `{"allow":[],"entries":{"codex":{"enabled":true}}}` | stable doctor: 0 asset lines | head `doctor --fix` then `doctor`: 1 line, `2 skills`; `plugins` subtree preserved |

Both arms were built with `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/build-all.mts cliStartup` and driven by the shipped launcher, each case in an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` and `HOME`. The base arm is frozen at `1342a4e`, an ancestor of this PR's base `dd89642`; the three touched production files are byte-identical between those two commits (`git diff` empty), so the base arm exercises exactly the base behavior of every changed line.

### Doctor scan, real `openclaw doctor`

Both arms report their own commit, so the cells cannot be confused:

```console
$ node openclaw.mjs --version
OpenClaw 2026.11.10 (1342a4e)     # base arm
OpenClaw 2026.11.10 (eb5e466)     # this head

$ OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=<isolated> HOME=<isolated> node openclaw.mjs doctor --non-interactive
# base, plugins: {"allow":[],"entries":{"codex":{"enabled":true}}}
(no "Doctor info" section at all - grep -c 'Personal Codex CLI assets found' => 0)

# this head, same config
┌  Doctor info ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  - Personal Codex CLI assets found (2 skills, 0 plugins, 0 config        │
│    files, 0 hook files) in <home>/.codex and <home>/.agents/skills;      │
│    native Codex-mode agents use isolated per-agent homes and will not    │
│    load them.                                                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

Counts across the six doctor configs are the first six rows of the table above: base `0 1 1 0 0 0`, head `1 1 1 0 0 0`; only the empty-allow-plus-entry cell changed.

### `/tools` inventory, real Gateway + real RPC

A real Gateway (`node openclaw.mjs gateway --port <port> --auth token ...`) served the cells, the session came from `sessions.create`, and each cell is a full `gateway call`. Five cells ran as config hot-reloads on one Gateway per arm; the `plugins disabled` cell ran as a cold Gateway start on both arms (its base notice only fires when `allow` is an array, which is why its input includes `allow: []`).

```console
$ node openclaw.mjs gateway call tools.effective --params '{"sessionKey":"agent:main:dashboard:..."}' --json

# base, plugins: {"allow":[],"entries":{"browser":{"enabled":false}}}
{"id":"browser-plugin-not-allowed","severity":"warning","message":"Browser is configured, but plugins.allow does not include browser. Add \"browser\" to plugins.allow or remove the restrictive plugin allowlist."}

# this head, same config
{"id":"browser-plugin-not-allowed","severity":"warning","message":"Browser is configured, but the browser plugin is disabled by plugin policy (disabled in config). Remove the plugin disable that applies to browser."}

# base, plugins: {"enabled":false,"allow":[]}  (cold start)
{"id":"browser-plugin-not-allowed","severity":"warning","message":"Browser is configured, but plugins.allow does not include browser. Add \"browser\" to plugins.allow or remove the restrictive plugin allowlist."}

# this head, same config (cold start)
{"id":"browser-plugin-not-allowed","severity":"warning","message":"Browser is configured, but the browser plugin is disabled by plugin policy (plugins disabled). Remove the plugin disable that applies to browser."}

# this head, plugins: {"deny":["browser"]}   (base printed no notice at all)
{"id":"browser-plugin-not-allowed","severity":"warning","message":"Browser is configured, but the browser plugin is disabled by plugin policy (blocked by denylist). Remove the plugin disable that applies to browser."}

# controls (browser enabled / allow:[] only / allow:["slack"] + entry on) - no notices on either arm
```

### OpenShell binding, real shipped `openshell worker configure`

Config: `plugins.deny: [" File-Transfer "]` plus an agent workspace binding (`agentId: main`, `remoteRoot: /sandbox/agent-main`) and the worker profile/model settings the command requires. The OpenShell sandbox peer is a synthetic executable that answers only the node-identity and workspace-check sandbox calls; every OpenClaw step — config snapshot, plugin policy decision, binding composition, config mutation — runs from the shipped bundle. No real OpenShell device is available locally.

```console
$ OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=<isolated> HOME=<isolated> node openclaw.mjs openshell worker configure demo-sandbox --worker-profile w1 --apply

# base (1342a4e): exit 0
# config file CHANGED: entries.file-transfer.enabled: true written, workspace
# binding and cloudWorkers profile applied despite the deny entry.

# this head (eb5e466): exit 1
Agent workspace binding requires File Transfer; preserve the existing plugin restriction and enable it explicitly before retrying.
# config file UNCHANGED (cmp against the pre-run copy: identical).
```

### Upgrade path, latest stable -> head on the same state

One state dir, config `plugins: {"allow":[],"entries":{"codex":{"enabled":true}}}`, the same two-skill `HOME` fixture throughout:

```console
$ openclaw --version                      # npm openclaw@2026.11.10
OpenClaw 2026.11.10 (6ea542f)
$ openclaw doctor --non-interactive       # stable: grep count => 0

$ node openclaw.mjs doctor --fix          # this head, migration entry, exit 0
$ node openclaw.mjs doctor --non-interactive
# grep count => 1 ("2 skills"); plugins subtree parsed-equal to the input
# ({"allow":[],"entries":{"codex":{"enabled":true}}}); both SKILL.md assets
# intact; no files removed.
```

### Built bundle form

The bundles the two arms actually executed:

```text
base  dist/codex-native-assets-*.mjs
  isCodexPluginConfigured(e){const t=e.plugins;if(t?.enabled===false)return false;const n=t?.allow;
  if(Array.isArray(n))return n.some(e=>normalizeOptionalLowercaseString(e)===`codex`); ... }

head  dist/codex-native-assets-*.mjs
  isCodexPluginConfigured(e){const t=normalizePluginsConfig(e.plugins);return resolveEffectiveEnableState({
  id:`codex`,origin:`bundled`,config:t,rootConfig:e,enabledByDefault:t.entries.codex!==void 0||t.allow.includes(`codex`)}).enabled}
```

### Focused tests

The new scenarios are folded into the existing cases, so the test line delta is -1 (`+19 / -20`):

```console
$ vitest run src/agents/tools-effective-inventory.test.ts src/commands/doctor/shared/codex-native-assets.test.ts extensions/openshell/src/worker-cli.test.ts
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  25 passed (25)
```

Red on base: with only the three production files reverted to base and the tests kept, exactly the four new scenarios fail:

```console
# base production files, this head's tests
 Test Files  3 failed (3)
      Tests  4 failed | 21 passed (25)
# failing: inventory deny row, inventory disabled-in-config row,
# codex empty-allow-plus-entry row, openshell padded-deny binding case
```

### What was not tested

The OpenShell binding has no real sandbox device here; the shipped run above uses a synthetic sandbox peer (disclosed in that section), backed by the red-on-base `worker-cli` test. Local verification ran the targeted vitest lanes and the shipped builds; the repository-wide typecheck runs in CI.

### Open PR collision check

Searched open PRs by file name and by changed-file list: `#199068` (roboclaw-bot) and `#194876` (saariuslystoned) both touch `src/agents/tools-effective-inventory.ts`, but only around the gateway/metadata scope in the middle of the file and around the notices assembly at the end; this change is confined to `buildToolInventoryNotices`, which neither edits. No open PR touches the other two files. Rechecked on 2026-11-26 against the current open-PR snapshot: `#205688`, `#205657` and `#205659` share no file with this change.

prs.title: refactor(subagents): check a Stop's caller authority once, then let the admitted kill finish
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When someone stops a sub-agent, OpenClaw kept re-asking during the Stop whether that caller still had authority over the run. The question came up again before each step, after the kill intent was already recorded, after the run was interrupted, and before the result was published. If the answer changed at any of those points, the Stop backed out with "ownership changed; retry".

That had two bad results:

- A Stop could do real work, such as aborting the child's run, and still report failure to the caller. Example: authority is revoked after the abort. The run is stopped, but the call rejects with the caller's revocation error.
- A Stop could undo itself. Stopping a parent's chat retires the parent turn that the Stop's authority came from. The collector kill then refused partway through, so `sessions.abort` reported that nothing was stopped and the collector stayed queued.

The repository rule (AGENTS.md, "Choose good compromises") is to check authority once, when work starts, and let a started request finish. Revocation applies to the next request. #202442 and #204249 already removed in-run authority re-checks elsewhere. Kill is the largest remaining place that still does it.

## User Impact

- A caller who loses control before the Stop selects its runs is refused, and nothing stops. This is unchanged.
- After that point, the Stop finishes and reports what it did, even if the caller loses control meanwhile or the Stop ends the parent turn that started it.
- The checks that this exact run and session incarnation are still the ones being stopped are unchanged. A kill never touches a successor run.
- `docs/tools/subagents/operations.md` ("Stopping") now states when authority is checked.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `withSubagentKillScope` owns admission. It checks the caller while selecting the run tree and once more right before running the kill. After that its `assertCurrent` checks only the registry write source, not the caller. It also stops calling the caller's `prepareRead`, because that read prepares the caller's authority check (the subagents tool's version calls `assertSelection()`). Each tree's own session and registry read preparation is unchanged. The descendant-refresh special case that let already-accepted outcomes past a revoked caller is deleted, because there is no revoked caller after admission.
- `mutateSubagentRunForKill` loses `declineRevokedCancellation` and its five call sites (three in preparation, two in the run phase). It also loses the `acceptance.callerFailure` paths and the post-claim branches that settled or released the claim after a revocation.
- `createSubagentKillAcceptance` drops `assertCallerCurrent` and its recorded caller failure. It keeps only native-owner checks when cancelling commands.
- The kill-settlement owner drops the caller check inside `markSubagentRunTerminated`. `assertCancellationCurrent` becomes `assertClaimCurrent` (the claimed row and session incarnation only).
- `settleSubagentKill` no longer re-asserts the caller after the kill. `killLatestSubagentRun` no longer re-asserts it while cancelling the run's commands.

Size: production code is +39 −149 across 5 files (tests +52 −64). Complexity from the same scanner (`scb-check`) before and after: `mutateSubagentRunForKill` CC 154 → 132, `withSubagentKillScope` CC 140 → 134, and the runtime's `cancellation` closure CC 40 → 35.

Not in this PR: the session-incarnation fence (`ownsSessionIncarnation`, `releaseChangedSession`) is still re-checked in flight. The kill claim already records `sessionId` and `lifecycleRevision`, so the next step makes the claim the single identity check. That changes what a session reset during a kill reports, so it gets its own PR and proof.

Open overlap: #194275 changes `subagent-control-kill-scope.ts` and `subagent-control-kill.ts`, and #189391 changes `subagent-control-kill-scope.ts`. Either will need a rebase.

## Evidence

- `subagent-control.concurrency.test.ts` "refuses a Stop revoked before admission and finishes one revoked %s":
  - Revoked while the tree is selected: the Stop is refused, nothing is aborted and nothing is interrupted.
  - Revoked after interruption or after abort: the Stop resolves `{ found: true, killed: true }`, the run is aborted, the admission is interrupted once, and no kill intent is left behind.
  - On main, the two "after" cases reject with the caller error, and in the "after abort" case the run is still aborted. They fail on main and pass here.
- `session-utils.queued-collector.test.ts`, scenario `sessions.abort exact=false parent-retired`: the Stop that retires its own parent turn now stops the collector (`respond` true, collector no longer queued).
- Other tests updated to the same contract. In each one, the cleanup and ordering assertions that are the test's real subject are unchanged:
  - `subagent-control.accepted-stop.test.ts`: an accepted Stop whose caller is revoked mid-settlement resolves and publishes `onResult` once instead of rejecting.
  - `subagent-control.commands.test.ts`: `postaccept-revoked` reports `ok`, and `late-revoked-evicted` no longer carries the revocation in its error. The cleanup failure still reports `error`.
  - `subagent-control.worker.test.ts`: a caller that retires after the kill claim commits gets a completed kill. A replaced session incarnation still releases the claim, because that identity check is kept.
  - `subagent-control.concurrency.test.ts` "an admitted Stop never waits on caller facts requested while …": caller facts are not read after admission.
- Before the change, the 26 kill-related test files passed 363/363 on main.
- After the change, run sequentially:
  - `src/agents/subagents`: 1,331 passed and 1 skipped. The only failures in that run were the 5 cases of the last concurrency test above, which was then rewritten; that file now passes 12/12.
  - The gateway and auto-reply abort, stop, kill, queued-collector and reset tests, plus the tool and kill callers: all passed (763 + 120 + 118 + 11 + 7).
- A first combined run had 6 gateway-server files fail in teardown with `ERR_SPAWN_BROKER_UNAVAILABLE` and no assertion failures. Those files pass when run alone (8 files, 70 tests).
- `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:test:src` are clean, as are oxfmt, oxlint on the changed files and `git diff --check`.
- Local autoreview, branch mode at P0–P2, with the unchanged kill capture, intent, types and session modules and the `subagents-tool`, `chat-abort-runtime` and `chat-abort-descendants` callers as source context: `scoped-clean`, no findings, confidence 0.84.
- Not exercised: a live Gateway Stop raced against a role change in a real channel. The proof is the in-process gateway and registry harness above.
- Follow-up `244964d`: PR CI's `checks-node-changed-compact-large-33` shard showed that two spawn production-boundary helpers still expected the old contract. They now expect admitted native Stops to finish: "separates native stop acceptance from caller revocation" (after interruption, already interrupted) and the `consumed-active-revoked` custody case, which reports `ok` with `killed: 1`. With main's production code those three fail, and they pass here. `subagent-spawn.production-boundary.test.ts` passes 140/141. The one failure, `preserves routed native Stop authority … (consumed-session)`, fails the same way with main's production code (`aborted` expected false, received true). It is the existing order-dependent failure on main described in #205482.
- CI run 45835338650 on `244964d`: the `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets` job ran for 47 minutes and stopped inside "Run baseline ratchets". The step never reported a result, and GitHub returns `BlobNotFound` for its log, so the runner was lost. Locally, `pnpm check:baseline-ratchets --base origin/main --no-merge-base` on the PR merged with current main passes every ratchet: max-lines, assertion-safety, session-identity, runtime-process-lifecycle, mock-exports, and test-lines (net −12 against a 400 allowance). Only the failed jobs were rerun, as an infrastructure recovery.

auto_merge.commit_message:
* refactor(subagents): check a Stop's caller authority once, then let the admitted kill finish

A subagent Stop re-checked its caller's authority before almost every step,
including after its kill intent was recorded and after the run was aborted.
A revocation in between made the Stop back out or report failure after the
work was done.

The kill scope now checks the caller while it selects the run tree and once
more at admission. After that only the claimed row and session incarnation
stay checked. This removes the per-run revocation decline path, the
acceptance caller-failure path and the post-kill caller re-assertions.

* test(subagents): expect admitted native Stops to finish after caller revocation

prs.title: fix(ci): keep browser PID tests stable on busy runners
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The browser PID test requires real HTTP discovery, a WebSocket upgrade, and a CDP reply to finish inside 100 ms even though it is checking PID matching. That ties the assertion to runner scheduling. The positive assertion failed in [the hourly Node extension job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45906150804/job/140203773994).

## User Impact

This is a maintainer-directed CI reliability repair. Production browser behavior is unchanged. The test still uses real loopback HTTP and WebSocket I/O and checks both matching and different PIDs.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the clock adapter already used by the replacement-browser test so native HTTP socket deadlines and JavaScript deadlines share one controlled clock. Keep the original 100 ms and 10 ms arguments, track both requests for cleanup, and require two SystemInfo replies so the negative case cannot pass because transport failed.

prs.title: improve: reduce memory when the catalog first captures plugin source
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the catalog first asks the broker to own a plugin source, the broker evaluates 216 additional files from the installed `@openclaw/fs-safe` package. The files total 1,454,020 bytes. This happens while attaching the owner, before the first request to create a source directory.

## User Impact

The catalog can keep its source owner alive with a smaller broker process. In a packaged Linux x64 fixture, median broker PSS after the first source request fell from 67,662 to 59,960 KiB. Operator configuration and filesystem permissions stay the same.

## Why This Change Was Made

The two broker attachment entry points already share private chunks. Bundle the filesystem code they use in that group. Native libraries and platform helper assets still resolve from the installed dependency. The logger and semver keep their runtime-selected exports. The normal compressed package grows by 65,127 bytes (124,125,394 → 124,190,521), with two additional private chunks. The global runtime, SDK and sealed workers keep their existing packaging.

Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/192547

## Evidence

Compared normal package builds from `3c6820c69e2a` and `35f1d307320a`. The standalone broker ran on Node 24.22.1, Linux x64, one CPU, 2 GiB RAM, no swap and no network. Counts come from a separate module-evaluation probe. Timing and PSS come from six fresh, uninstrumented processes in stock/changed/changed/stock/stock/changed order. All six created and released real source directories and joined on close. [Testbox allocation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45919599779)

| Broker stage | Stock PSS (KiB) | Changed PSS (KiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Ready | 49,680 | 49,618 |
| Source owner attached | 65,876 | 57,962 |
| First source created | 67,662 | 59,960 |
| First source released | 67,972 | 60,050 |
| After warm cycles | 70,940 | 62,766 |

- Ready already evaluated 13 external fs-safe files in both builds. Attaching the stock owner evaluated 216 more, including the `advanced` entry. The changed owner added zero. Both evaluated the same 33 external logger files. The SQLite entry was absent from this workload.
- Median cold attachment took 130.873 → 47.636 ms. First source creation took 7.076 → 6.675 ms. Each child then warmed up for 10 cycles and timed 160 source-create/release cycles. Median per-run p50/p95/p99 were 0.805/1.155/1.850 ms stock and 0.826/1.122/2.049 ms changed. The p99 rose 0.199 ms. Across runs the p99 ranged from 1.517 to 28.603 ms stock and 1.798 to 27.287 ms changed. Median broker CPU was 15 ticks per 160 cycles in both arms (100 Hz). These data support the cold attachment and memory result. Warm throughput and whole-Gateway memory remain unproven.
- Both normal packages passed plugin-first, SQLite-first, and SQLite-only lifecycles. The sentinel snapshot remained readable after renaming the installed dist tree. Existing resource cleanup, sealing and process exit succeeded.
- Both passed the real catalog owner/source/release sequence on Bun 1.4.4. A separate asset probe exercised the installed optional Linux N-API binary from a relocated package, including a native canonical-path operation. It verified the Windows helper asset path and bytes on Linux. The changed probe exposed existing private bindings in disposable copies of the emitted chunks. Windows execution was outside this run. Node and Bun selected their respective external logger exports.
- The package, shared group, resource retirement and relocated-runtime tests passed, along with targeted formatting and lint. The new group contract assertions failed against stock.

prs.title: improve: set automation hours in the schedule builder
prs.body:
> [!WARNING]
> **Do not land.** Still in progress and under discussion. Talk to @vyctorbrzezowski.

## What Problem This Solves

The automation editor gives you an hours picker in the schedule and a second hours setting under Advanced. A cron job can even show “all day” in the schedule while Advanced restricts it, and the two time-zone inputs can disagree.

## User Impact

Use **Between hours** and one **Time zone** field in the schedule builder for interval and cron jobs. The start is included and the end is excluded: 08:00–22:00 does not include 22:00. Overnight windows work too.

**Existing jobs:** No jobs are rewritten, paused, or deleted on upgrade, and no Doctor action is required. Existing windows still apply on resave, including to forced runs. If a saved cron job already uses different zones for its schedule and window, the editor keeps both and explains the difference. Editing the one time-zone field applies the new zone to both.

## Why This Change Was Made

New cron windows use hour ranges when the schedule can express them directly. Elapsed intervals, such as every 45 minutes, keep their cadence and use the existing runtime window. Minute-level windows also keep their runtime restriction when a cron hour range cannot express them. The Gateway API, CLI, agent tool and stored job format are unchanged: translating existing runtime gates to cron ranges would change when a manual run is allowed, so this removes the duplicate editor path rather than migrating jobs in Doctor.

Expected sibling overlap: automation editor and Advanced settings layout, the schedule docs, and editor-save and browser test fixtures. This PR does not change the other settings or the runtime policy contracts.

## Evidence

I merged main at `2ab7b31a13d95bbbb62596679b130445c4c9d3d1` without rebasing and resolved the six conflicted files. The merge commit is `e5824d429191d9eff60394d0c5ddd060848dd36e`.

I reproduced both reported regressions in the actual automation page with fixture Gateway RPCs: four supported schedule kinds could not enable hours, and cloning hid the preserved split time zone. All five cases failed before the fixes. With the fixes, all 109 tests in five focused files passed locally: the page, view, schedule sentence, editor-save, and form-validation suites. I also passed `pnpm tsgo:ui`, targeted lint, formatting, the English-copy baseline check, and the diff check against merged main. The committed tree matches the tested tree. These are local harness checks, not real-Gateway or upgrade proof.

The interrupted test attempt ended with SIGTERM/exit 143; the completed replacement run exited 0. Local autoreview of the complete candidate against the pinned main base could not start because the selected Codex installation could not execute inside its required read-only sandbox. I left review permissions unchanged. No clean independent-review result is claimed, and I did not request a hosted re-review.

Simplification: the shared picker remains the sole hours control for every supported schedule, and the existing clone source supplies the split-zone explanation. No new state owner or compatibility layer was added. Against merged main: production +247/-232, tests and test support +180/-29, docs +2/-0.

Still missing: publicly inspectable annotated before/after screenshots; real-Gateway save/reopen proof for the consolidated controls and preserved runtime windows; latest-stable upgrade/data-compatibility proof; a base-red/head-green real-runtime comparison; and full final-head CI. The five local red/green cases do not replace those checks. This stays a draft under the existing do-not-land hold.

prs.title: fix(android): honor bounded server retryAfterMs reconnect hints
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a Gateway refuses a connect attempt with a retryable error containing `retryAfterMs` (for example while starting up or backing off), the Android app ignores `retryAfterMs` and reconnects using only its local exponential backoff schedule. That can either retry too aggressively against a busy/starting Gateway or ignore explicit server-side pacing.

## User Impact

User impact: Android reconnects respect server-provided `retryAfterMs` hints (clamped to 1–60 seconds with positive jitter so retries are never shortened below the server's window), while explicit user-initiated reconnects and network-restore retries still interrupt the wait immediately.

## Why This Change Was Made

Parses `error.retryAfterMs` onto `GatewaySession.ErrorShape`, computes `gatewayConnectRetryDelayMs` only for `retryable == true` errors clamped to `1_000..60_000 ms` (with up to +20% jitter capped at 60 s), and waits for `maxOf(gatewayReconnectDelayMs(attempt), gatewayConnectRetryDelayMs(error))` inside the existing `awaitGatewayReconnectSignal` select loop.

## Evidence

- Verified unit tests covering `retryable`-only parsing, 1–60 s bounds, non-shortening jitter, server-delay honoring on connect failure, and immediate interruption by `retryAfterNetworkRestore()` / `reconnect()` (`./gradlew :app:testPlayDebugUnitTest --tests "ai.openclaw.app.gateway.GatewayReconnectDelayTest" --tests "ai.openclaw.app.gateway.GatewaySessionReconnectTest.retryableConnectFailureHonorsServerDelayAndExplicitReconnectInterruptsIt"`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`).

prs.title: fix(slack): apply allowBots to bot message edits and deletes
prs.body:
Closes #206012

Thanks @lockhartheavyindustries for the queue-cap log trail.

## What Problem This Solves

`allowBots` was enforced on new bot messages but not on bot-authored edits and deletes. Those subtype events skip `prepareSlackMessage`, so the monitor authorized them by channel and sender allowlist only and enqueued a system event. An app that keeps editing its own cards — the GitHub for Slack app refreshing PR/CI cards, for example — could fill a session's system-event queue under `allowBots: "mentions"` until further events were refused.

## User Impact

Bot edits and deletes now follow the same policy as new bot messages:

- `allowBots: false` drops bot-authored subtype events.
- `allowBots: true` (the default) keeps the current behavior.
- `allowBots: "mentions"` admits an edit or delete only when the text addresses the agent the way ordinary preparation does: a configured mention pattern, an explicit `<@botUserId>` mention, or a subteam mention whose membership includes the bot. DMs also count as addressed.

Human edits and deletes are untouched, and bot messages that explicitly mention the agent still produce system events.

## Why This Change Was Made

The subtype branch now resolves the same setting the ordinary path resolves through a shared helper: channel config, then account config, then the global Slack setting, defaulting to `true`. Both call sites use it, so the precedence cannot drift. A helper, `resolveSlackBotSubtypeAdmission`, mirrors the ordinary gate's shape (`false` drops, `true` allows, `"mentions"` requires an address) and keeps the decision testable without a Bolt harness. It reuses the ordinary pipeline's mention contracts, `matchesMentionWithExplicit` over the configured mention patterns and `isSlackSubteamMentionForBot` for user-group membership, instead of maintaining a narrower subtype-only list.

Mention matching uses the edited message's new text, including top-level edits where Slack omits `thread_ts`; a mention added by an edit counts, and one removed by an edit does not. A thread-root deletion arrives as a Slackbot `message_changed` tombstone rather than `message_deleted`, so authorship and the mention check fall back to the previous message there; otherwise bot deletions on thread roots would skip the gate.

Mention detection here reuses the contracts the ordinary pipeline already applies: configured mention patterns, an explicit bot user mention, and subteam membership resolved through `isSlackSubteamMentionForBot` with the same short-lived membership cache as preparation. The gate runs only for messages carrying `bot_id` or `subtype: "bot_message"`, so human edits keep their existing authorization path.

## Evidence

The helper tests cover each `allowBots` value, mention and non-mention text, unknown bot user ids, DM admission, top-level edits whose new text differs from the previous message, and Slackbot tombstones. Handler tests drive the registered Slack events through the real subtype branch and assert both directions: an unmentioned bot edit, delete, or tombstone is dropped, a mentioned one is queued, and a bot edit in a DM is queued under `"mentions"`. Account-level fallback and channel-over-account precedence are covered too. The P2 repair adds subteam membership (included and excluded), a configured mention pattern, and the matching delete case at both the helper and registered-handler levels.

```
CI=1 ./node_modules/.bin/vitest run extensions/slack/src/monitor/events extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/subteam-mentions.test.ts extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/prepare.bot-messages.test.ts extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/prepare.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
  Test Files  12 passed (12)
  Tests       276 passed (276)
```

Formatting, scoped `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` are clean. See Real behavior proof below for the isolated Gateway run; a live Slack workspace with real Slack transport was not exercised.

## Merge danger

Two-way door: a revert restores the earlier behavior of admitting every bot edit and delete. No configuration, schema, or stored state changes.

## Real behavior proof

**What ran.** Three isolated Gateway processes ran the shipped Slack extension in HTTP mode: the real Bolt receiver with webhook signature verification, the real message event handler, the real subtype admission path, the real system-event queue, and a real agent turn. Each Gateway loaded `dist/extensions/slack` built from the tested revision, confirmed by the plugin-load log line and `dist/build-info.json`. Every run used its own `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, config, and loopback ports.

Tested revisions:

- `e0e0b6d19` - base before the PR (red-before for the original defect).
- `94b359b8` - previous PR head (red-before for the P2 finding).
- `1be9d94fd` - this head (green).

**What is stubbed.** Slack itself was a local HTTP stub. It answered Slack Web API calls (`auth.test`, `users.info`, `conversations.info`, `usergroups.users.list`, `chat.postMessage`) and accepted locally generated, HMAC-signed Events API POSTs. The model was a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint that recorded each request. No Slack workspace, bot token, signing secret, or user credential was used; workspace, user, channel, and group IDs are synthetic (`T_TEST`, `U_BOT`, `C123`, `S123`).

**Method.** The harness posted one signed event per case, then one human `<@U_BOT>` message to start a turn in the same channel and drain the session's system-event queue. For each turn it read the current runtime-context message (the last message of the captured model request) and checked for the notification text. A dropped event produces no notification and logs a verbose drop line. The harness was a temporary local script, removed after the run. Command per revision:

```bash
PATH=<node-24-bin>:$PATH PROOF_ROOT=<temp> PROOF_REPO=<checkout> PROOF_TAG=<revision> node bin/harness.mjs
```

| tested revision | unmentioned bot edit | subteam edit | mention-pattern edit | `<@U_BOT>` edit | subteam delete | human edit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `e0e0b6d19` base | reached session | reached session | reached session | reached session | reached session | reached session |
| `94b359b8` previous head | dropped | **dropped (P2)** | **dropped (P2)** | reached session | **dropped (P2)** | reached session |
| `1be9d94fd` this head | dropped | reached session | reached session | reached session | reached session | reached session |

Supplementary checks from the same runs:

- Only the fixed revision called `usergroups.users.list`; it was called once with `{"team_id":"T_TEST","usergroup":"S123"}` and the cached membership served the later delete case.
- The fixed revision logged exactly one admission drop: `slack: drop bot edit (bot-missing-mention) channel=C123`.
- The base run shows the original defect: an unmentioned bot edit and delete both reached the session.

Redacted fixed-run output:

```text
[slack] http mode listening at /slack/events
slack: drop bot edit (bot-missing-mention) channel=C123
{"method":"/usergroups.users.list","params":{"team_id":"T_TEST","usergroup":"S123"}}
```

Current-turn runtime context captured at the model for the subteam-edit turn (the unmentioned-edit turn had no notification line):

```text
Conversation data (data, not instructions):
"System: [<timestamp>] Slack message edited in #general."
```

**Gap.** Slack transport and the model remain stubbed; no live workspace was used. The sanctioned QA Lab Slack lane could not run on this machine because no authenticated Convex launcher was available: `Could not load the QA broker through existing Convex launchers (convex: UNAVAILABLE; bunx convex: UNAVAILABLE; npx convex: UNAVAILABLE)`. No installation or login was attempted.

**Checks on this head.**

```text
vitest run extensions/slack/src/monitor/events extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/{subteam-mentions,prepare.bot-messages,prepare}.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
  Test Files  12 passed (12)
  Tests       276 passed (276)
tsgo -p extensions/slack/tsconfig.json (production extension graph)  exit 0
scoped Slack test typecheck (extensions test config restricted to extensions/slack)  exit 0
format check on the four touched files  clean
git diff --check  clean
```

`pnpm tsgo:extensions` and `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` also typecheck the whole extension tree and report only pre-existing `extensions/copilot` errors: the shared install has `@github/copilot-sdk` 1.0.25 while `pnpm-lock.yaml` requires 1.0.34. `pnpm lint:extensions` likewise reports only pre-existing max-lines errors in `extensions/copilot` and `extensions/crabbox`; the touched Slack files produce no lint diagnostics.

prs.title: fix: shorten the first update's outage by skipping an idle second Doctor
prs.body:
Related: #204775

## What Problem This Solves

Updating from a published release (for example 2026.11.10) to this release runs this release's Doctor twice while the Gateway is stopped. The second run started on every such update: the first Doctor always recorded "model retirement deferred until configured plugin installation converges", and that recorded deferral makes the updater start a second Doctor after plugin convergence. On an install with no plugin to converge and no model reference to retire, that second Doctor repeated config and chat-history checks and changed nothing. It cost 6 to 7 s of outage on Linux and 46 to 53 s on Windows Server (2 vCPU).

## User Impact

A first update from a published package no longer runs the idle second Doctor, so the Gateway is back sooner. The repairs and migrations are the same: the resulting schema versions, config, database row counts and a chat turn through the restarted Gateway match the build without this change. When retirement or stale plugin config repair does have work, or a plugin install can still change during convergence, the update waits and runs the second Doctor as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The model retirement owner (`runDoctorRepairSequence`) already knows, at the moment it records the deferral, everything the second Doctor would decide on: the second Doctor starts from the config the first one writes, and with no install record and no pending install repair the plugin inventory cannot change in between. So before recording the deferral it now runs the three repairs the second pass would run (stale plugin config, implicit OpenAI primary, stale model references) on a private copy of the candidate config, in the same order. It records the deferral only if one of them would change or warn, or if convergence can still change plugins: any install record, install repair change, warning or notice, a failed plugin install, or explicit model replacements. No new stored field, flag or protocol: the post-core decision (`completePostCorePluginUpdate`) keeps reading the existing ledger step, which simply is not written when there is nothing to wait for.

Cost: the private-copy check adds about 0.5 s inside the first Doctor (the "Config repairs" phase went from under 0.3 s to 0.8 s in the cells).

**Update behavior.** The installed 2026.11.10 runs the update. With the Gateway stopped it calls this release twice: `infra/update-migrated-finalize.worker.js --doctor` (the first Doctor, through 2026.11.10's `runPackageUpdateDoctor`), then `--post-core`, which runs this release's `openclaw update` continuation. This change is in the first call: the first Doctor no longer records the deferral when nothing waits on convergence. The second call reads that ledger and, with plugins unchanged, no longer starts the second `--doctor` (and its capability probe). Nothing in the installed updater changes; any published driver that hands off to this release's post-core gets the shorter stop on its first update. Updates driven by this release's own path are unaffected unless they set the package-swap marker, and then the same rule applies.

## Where the first update's outage goes (Linux, before)

Installed published 2026.11.10 (npm global, systemd user Gateway), candidate `main` packed as an unpublished version, `/readyz` probed every 250 ms, run record step times, ms-stamped updater stderr. 4 GiB agent database with 1 MiB/s of writes while serving (cell G-base.1):

| Inside the stop | Who runs it | Seconds |
|---|---|---|
| Service stop, post-stop checks | installed 2026.11.10 | 0.5 |
| Database snapshot | installed 2026.11.10 | 14.7 |
| Config snapshot and Doctor setup | installed 2026.11.10 | 5.2 |
| **Doctor 1**: `--doctor`, called by 2026.11.10 | this release | **57.8** |
| of which: schema admission 3.7, maintenance begin 3.7, database migrations 20.8, config flow 8.1, contributions 10.2, maintenance finish 4.0 | | |
| Handoff: `--post-core`, called by 2026.11.10 | this release | 6.4 |
| Plugin convergence, config validation, readiness lint | this release | 4.2 |
| **Doctor 2**: retirement-only `--doctor`, called by this release's post-core | this release | **6.7** |
| Service reinstall and restart | this release | 3.2 |
| Gateway start to ready | this release | 7 |
| **Not serving** | | **107.2** |

Doctor runs twice inside the stop on Linux too, as on Windows. Doctor 1 is the real migration. Doctor 2 ran only because of the recorded deferral: plugins were unchanged (`finalize:plugins:0`, retirement-only selection) and it changed nothing.

**Ranked by seconds the new release can remove without the installed updater:**

1. Doctor 2 (this PR): 6 to 7 s on Linux at any store size, 46 to 53 s on Windows (its section times there: config flow 13 to 17 s, chat history 20 to 21 s).
2. Repeated chat-history scan in Doctor 2: covered by 1. The existing scan-reuse receipt (#177933) cannot help this hop: Doctor 1's receipt goes to the installed 2026.11.10 parent, not to this release's post-core.
3. Doctor 1 itself (21 to 59 s): database migrations are the schema change itself, and config flow and contributions run once per update. I found nothing there that repeats work or that a later step could prove done, so it is not changed here.

## Evidence

Driver for every cell: published 2026.11.10 from npm. Base candidate: `main` (red at `3495c164737`, comparison base at `fcc9a0648c2`), packed as 2026.11.13. Head candidate: this PR's production code at `474dce4fafa`, packed as 2026.11.14 (later commits on the branch change one test and merge `main`; no Doctor or update path file moved, checked with `git diff --name-only`). Every run: `openclaw update --yes --json` exit 0, run record `succeeded`, Gateway serving the candidate afterwards.

prs.title: fix: report the default deep research runtime accurately
prs.body:
Closes #205544

## What Problem This Solves

Deep Research's capabilities answer says `direct-provider`, although ordinary portable requests select `isolated-agent-runtime`. An agent checking capabilities before a default research job is therefore told to expect the wrong execution route.

## User Impact

Capabilities now report the default accurately. Explicit `requiredAuthMode: "oauth"` requests retain their direct-provider route and OAuth-only constraint. No execution, credential, billing, or configuration policy changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The routing change in #177228 left the older capability constant behind. Re-auditing the registered tool, job owner, portable adapter, and host completion contract on pinned main confirmed that the metadata owner—not the router—needs the fix.

Kept this small branch and reconciled current main in place; rebuilding it would not improve the fix. Applied `pr-simplify`: one production-line replacement, one field added to the existing registered-tool assertion, and documentation of the default/OAuth distinction without repeating the exception. Existing default, OAuth-only, and no-direct-fallback tests are reused. No new test cases, helpers, comments, limits, or runtime branches.

Diff against the pinned base: **production +1/−1; tests +1/−1; docs +12/−10** (3 files, net +2 lines).

## Evidence

Audit base: `df720d5644b8e6b3a82ebfef32b7349fcc92c240`. Published head: `10ab65a1542a8d3c1d50ec843d8334b71f5cb93b`.

**Actual built backend, no mock Gateway:** built both baseline and candidate with `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/build-all.mts qaRuntime` (58.6s / 55.4s). Used the built CLI's baseline setup and foreground Gateway in separate temporary profiles, with token authentication and loopback ports. Both reached readiness. The same authenticated `POST /tools/invoke` request, `{"tool":"deep_research","args":{"action":"capabilities"},"sessionKey":"main"}`, returned HTTP 200:

```text
Baseline response.details.portable:
{"runtime":"direct-provider","nativeFunctionCallingRequired":false}

Candidate response.details.portable:
{"runtime":"isolated-agent-runtime","nativeFunctionCallingRequired":false}
```

Both Gateway processes exited 0; their listeners closed and disposable state was removed. This proves the capabilities endpoint, **not a model-backed research job**. The backend build profile is not a full release/declaration build.

**Regression and local checks:**
- On the pinned baseline implementation, the registered-tool/routing pair returned **1 failed, 7 passed**, failing specifically on the wrong runtime value. On the candidate, the full plugin command `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/test-extension.mts deep-research --maxWorkers=1` passed **105 tests in 10 files**, 59.18s Vitest duration. These tests use fixture runtime I/O.
- Changed registered-tool file: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/deep-research/index.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: **2 passed**, 41.38s Vitest / 44.05s wrapper wall time; the changed capabilities case took 163ms, with cold worker compilation dominating. Hosted CI seconds are unavailable.
- Targeted lint, extension production/test typechecks, format, and whitespace checks passed.
- Bound Auto Review, local candidate against the pinned base, **P0–P3**: `scoped-clean`, zero findings.

**Aggregate check is not green:** `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --staged --base df720d5644b8e6b3a82ebfef32b7349fcc92c240 --timed` exited 1. Its max-lines/env guard could not resolve ancestry in the managed shallow checkout; the same guard passed separately with its supported `--no-merge-base` option against the exact prepared base. Remaining reported failures:
- Changelog attribution at `CHANGELOG/2026.11.10.md:8130`.
- Eight unused exports across the Crabbox/Slack test support, model-catalog publisher, operator-role policy, project access, and roles UI. Every reported owning file and both scanners were byte-identical to the pinned base; the patch changes no imports or exports. This is source attribution, not a separately executed baseline full-tree scan. Unrelated files and safeguards were left unchanged.

**Not checked:** no real default portable model job, OAuth-provider job, entitlement, or billing qualification was run. The sandbox has no authorized live-model binding; the configured remote runner failed preflight, and no lease was allocated. These unchanged model-execution paths are not claimed as observed proof.

**Hosted review and CI:** [ClawSweeper revision 2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205647#issuecomment-7178895481) reviewed `10ab65a1542a8d3c1d50ec843d8334b71f5cb93b`: **Diamond (5/6)** overall, proof, and patch quality; **zero actionable findings; proof sufficient (terminal)**. prs.title: fix(subagents): notify the parent agent when Stop cancels sub-agents
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a person presses Stop in the Control UI (or the macOS app that hosts it) while the agent itself is idle but its sub-agents are still working, the app sends a session-wide `sessions.abort`. That Stop also cancels every running sub-agent of the session, which is the documented behavior. But canceled children never deliver a completion, and nothing else tells the parent agent what happened, so the agent keeps waiting for results that will never come, or later sees only bare process-exit failures. An orchestrator running several long sub-agents loses hours of work with no trace of why.

## Why This Change Was Made

Stop keeps its current meaning; the defect is the silence. Every explicit Stop that cancels sub-agents now queues one system notice for the parent session. It names the canceled sub-agents, says the Stop was deliberate and what kind it was, and tells the agent not to restart the work unless the user asks:

> An explicit session Stop from a connected app canceled 2 running sub-agents: slow-a, slow-b. They won't report back. Check their sessions before relying on any partial work, and don't restart them unless the user asks.

For a single sub-agent the sentence is singular ("It won't report back. Check its session…"). Empty labels are skipped, and names beyond the first ten are counted ("slow-a and 2 more").

- New `src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-stop-notice.ts` builds the notice and enqueues it through the existing system-event owner (`enqueueSystemEvent`). Zero kills queue nothing; labels are normalized, empty ones dropped, and at most 10 are named.
- The Gateway cancellation owner, `abortControlledSubagents`, calls it once per request after the cascade settles, when the caller passes an explicit `stopSource`: session-wide `sessions.abort` (`client-session`, "An explicit session Stop from a connected app"), exact-run `chat.abort` / `sessions.abort` (`client-run`, "An explicit Stop of your turn"). An exact-run `sessions.abort` either stops an embedded run directly or forwards to the `chat.abort` handler; both paths pass `client-run`. A session-wide `sessions.abort` that lands on an active embedded run takes the same turn-scoped path, so its notice reads as a Stop of that turn.
- Chat `/stop` (`stopSubagentsForRequester`) uses the same helper (`channel-user`, "A user /stop command"). It already replied "Stopped N sub-agents" to the person; now the agent learns it too.
- The notice is a queued system event: it doesn't start a turn and doesn't touch the stable prompt prefix; the parent's next turn reads it.
- Docs: `docs/tools/subagents/operations.md` ("Stopping").

No protocol, schema or config change. Which sub-agents a Stop selects is unchanged.

## User Impact

After an explicit Stop, the parent agent's next turn says which sub-agents were canceled and by what kind of Stop, so it stops waiting for them, can inspect their sessions, and does not restart work a person just stopped. Non-explicit cancellations (shutdown, timeouts) are unchanged.

Not in this PR: whether the Control UI should offer a session-wide Stop (or map Escape to it) when only sub-agents are running. That is a product decision and is left for a follow-up.

## Evidence

- Regression test: `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.abort-cascade.test.ts` "tells the requester's next turn which children a session/exact run Stop canceled" — red on the base, green with the fix. `src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-stop-notice.test.ts` covers the singular sentence, an empty label, one name with more remaining, and two names with more remaining.
- Consumer tests: all `chat.abort*`, `sessions.abort*`, `agent.abort*` suites in `src/gateway/server-methods` plus `subagent-control.test.ts` and the auto-reply abort tests pass (32 files on the final head). oxlint and oxfmt clean on touched files; `git diff --check` clean.
- End to end, isolated Gateway (own state and port), real agent on a real model (`openai/gpt-6.1-sol` through the Codex runtime): the parent spawns two sub-agents that run `sleep 900`, ends its turn, then the script sends exactly what the Control UI Stop sends when no local run id is known: `sessions.abort {key, clearQueued: true, userInitiated: true}`. Both runs: the sub-agents are killed and their processes are gone. Then the parent is asked whether its sub-agents are still running.
  - Base: "There is no system notice about their running status in this turn."
  - Fix: quoted the notice verbatim and answered that they were canceled.
  - This run used the earlier notice wording (it said "cancelled" and suggested spawning replacements). The wording was revised after review and was not rerun end to end; the unit and Gateway tests above cover the final text.
- Local review: autoreview (Codex) on the committed branch range against `origin/main`, P0 and P2 thresholds: no findings (the reviewer saw the diff only). I checked by hand that the two `sessions.abort` branches are exclusive, so one request queues one notice.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Commands such as `openclaw infer model run` load channel and web capability code while selecting model credentials. A short-lived CLI process pays for those imports even when it only uses a model provider.

## User Impact

Model, image, video and media commands can select model credentials independently of channel and web discovery. They use the same configured credential paths, including custom request headers, proxy TLS and request TLS. No configuration change is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The model credential paths are a fixed list. Model-only callers now import that list through a small module which creates a fresh set for each caller. Commands that combine model and other credentials reuse the same list and keep their existing discovery behavior.

## Evidence

- With the same pinned esbuild compiler and Node 24 target, the model command's emitted dynamic import selected a target module with 18 direct static imports on the parent and zero on this change. This measures the compiled module in isolation. Packaged startup time remains unmeasured.
- Compared the candidate getter with the parent definition at runtime. All 13 IDs matched in order, and clearing one returned set left the next call intact.
- Added a regression test that throws if model target selection imports channel, web fetch or web search discovery. The test verifies the full set after mutating the prior result.
- At `7067ab1f3251`, PR-shaped CI selected the import regression and all selected Node test jobs passed. Its mock-factory guard flagged five test factories and the packaged build job was skipped. The dependency check also reported unused symbols outside this change. [Initial CI run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45913760861)
- The test-only correction at `5729b04b9faa` uses the real getter in model config tests, documents four intentional mock boundaries and removes two old mock allowances. The repository's mock-factory scanner reproduced five new findings on the published parent and zero on the correction for the affected mocks. Formatting and whitespace checks passed. The full mock-factory ratchet passed on the corrected head. The five focused suites passed all 152 tests.
- The corrected head passed `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` on Linux with Node 24.22.1. The Testbox command exited zero and the one-shot lease stopped after completion. An optional probe of the final packaged dependency graph did not follow the generated re-export, so there is no measured package-byte or startup-time delta. [Testbox workflow](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45918285003)
- In the separately compiled test-worker distribution, the real model command selected a re-export and its implementation. The entire static dependency closure was two files totaling 982 bytes. Importing that compiled entry returned 13 independent targets.
- Local autoreview covered the full staged range from `eb0faf79a5be` through the contents of `5729b04b9faa` at priorities P0–P3, with zero actionable findings. Local ClawSweeper was unavailable because its installation could not resolve TypeScript.
